title: Kentucky Guardsmen Sharpen Capabilities Alongside NATO Partners
text: Ocean Rescue U.S. Air Force pararescuemen assigned to the Kentucky Air National Guard's 123rd Special Tactics Squadron jump from a C-130J Super Hercules aircraft into the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Scotland Aug. 18, 2026. The airmen are conducting open-ocean rescue training with members of the Kentucky Guard’s 165th Airlift Squadron and the British Royal Navy's 814 Naval Air Squadron. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.41 MB ) Credit: Dale Greer, Air Force VIRIN: 260818-Z-VT419-9059 Airmen assigned to the Kentucky Air National Guard enhanced their global capabilities while training alongside NATO partners from the United Kingdom and Canada in Scotland this summer. The guardsmen deployed four C-130J Super Hercules aircraft, 62,000 pounds of equipment and 60 personnel to Glasgow Prestwick Airport in South Ayrshire, Scotland, Aug. 14-22. While there, they conducted specialized fueling operations, low-level formation flying and rapid-reaction aircraft launches to maintain combat mission certifications. The airmen also completed maritime equipment and personnel airdrops, including two open-ocean rescue scenarios with a helicopter unit assigned to the British Royal Navy. "The deployment was designed to accomplish a large amount of C-130J continuation and tactical training while taking advantage of an unfamiliar overseas operating environment and opportunities to work directly with allied partners," said Air Force Lt. Col. Nick Reinke, the mission commander and a C-130 pilot assigned to the 165th Airlift Squadron. He added that while many of the individual training events could be conducted in the U.S., it is much harder to reproduce an unfamiliar environment. Super Hercules A U.S. Air Force C-130J Super Hercules aircraft assigned to the Kentucky Air National Guard's 165th Airlift Squadron flies a low-level sortie as part of a five-ship formation along the coast of Scotland Aug. 19, 2026. The unit is supporting a weeklong joint training exercise with the Kentucky Air Guard's 123rd Special Tactics Squadron and the British Royal Navy's 814th Naval Air Squadron. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.53 MB ) Credit: Dale Greer, Air Force VIRIN: 260819-Z-VT419-9732 "At home station, crews know the airspace, air traffic control procedures, airfields, support agencies and local practices," Reinke said. "In Scotland, even something as routine as a proficiency circuit required crews to understand and coordinate with a different [air traffic control] system." Reinke said coordination with host nation agencies was critical to the exercise's success. "That forces crews to solve the kinds of interoperability, communication, planning and adaptation problems they encounter when operating globally. Worldwide capability is more than simply being able to fly across the Atlantic. It means arriving with the people and equipment needed to operate, understanding an unfamiliar airspace and support structure, integrating with allied forces, adapting when weather or circumstances change the plan, and continuing to accomplish the mission." Reinke added that the deployment also underscored the importance of relationships. The Kentucky unit, based in Louisville, worked closely with civilian support agencies at Glasgow Prestwick Airport to complete specialized fueling operations, during which a C-130J was refueled while its engines were still running. Reinke said this "hot pit" method validated the airport's ability to support the technique and provided practical experience to host-nation fuel personnel. "That partnership leaves behind a more capable location for follow-on and allied forces in the future, rather than the benefit ending when our deployment ended," he noted. One of the deployment's key accomplishments was a five-ship formation flight, conducted with four Kentucky aircraft and one C-130J from the Royal Canadian Air Force. "The Canadian aircraft commander was actually a U.S. Marine Corps exchange pilot," Reinke said. "That meant our mission planning and briefing had to reconcile U.S. Air Force, Royal Canadian Air Force and U.S. Marine Corps procedures and terminology to make sure everyone had the same understanding before execution. That is exactly the kind of interoperability that is difficult to simulate." Mission Lands A U.S. Air Force C-130J Super Hercules aircraft assigned to the Kentucky Air National Guard's 165th Airlift Squadron lands at Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Prestwick, Scotland, after completing a five-ship formation flight along the coast of Scotland Aug. 19, 2026. The unit is supporting a weeklong joint training exercise in conjunction with the Kentucky Air Guard's 123rd Special Tactics Squadron and the British Royal Navy's 814th Naval Air Squadron. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.4 MB ) Credit: Dale Greer, Air Force VIRIN: 260819-Z-VT419-9269 The deployment's other main focus was open-ocean rescue. The scenario required a U.S. Air Force C-130 crew to locate a stranded airman floating in a life raft on the Atlantic Ocean, miles from shore. Loadmasters then airdropped an inflatable motorboat near the victim, and three special tactics airmen used precision jumpmaster techniques to parachute into the ocean, deploy the boat and provide first aid. Once complete, they coordinated with the Royal Navy's 814 Naval Air Squadron to execute helicopter hoist operations and extract the victim as the C-130 provided overwatch. "The integration with the Royal Navy was one of the highlights of the exercise," Reinke said. "It allowed our pararescue personnel and C-130J crews to integrate fixed-wing airdrop, maritime rescue, rotary-wing insertion and recovery, and on-scene command and control with a NATO partner." A pararescue flight chief for the special tactics team described the operating environment in Scotland as "vastly different" from training locations in the United States. "It's a lot colder here, and the salt water is an unusual factor for us," he said. "The Royal Navy also uses different geolocation methods, and they have different tactics and techniques than we typically employ." He noted that the Royal Navy's helicopter, a Merlin Mk2, generates substantially more rotor wash than the UH-60 Black Hawk. "Those are the kinds of things you don't anticipate, but we were able to work through them and figure out what worked best for their guys and for us," the airman said. "We had to be flexible on the spot to get the mission done." Royal Navy Capt. James Hall said the exercise provided valuable opportunities for the Merlin Mk2 force to enhance capabilities outside of its normal role in antisubmarine warfare. Inspection Watch U.S. Air Force Tech. Sgt. Michael Newton, a loadmaster assigned to the Kentucky Air National Guard's 165th Airlift Squadron, observes the preflight inspection of a C-130J Super Hercules aircraft at Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Prestwick, Scotland, Aug. 19, 2026. The aircraft is one of four deployed from Kentucky for a weeklong joint field training exercise with members of the British Royal Navy and the Canadian Royal Air Force. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.57 MB ) Credit: Dale Greer, Air Force VIRIN: 260819-Z-VT419-9062 "Exercises such as this, conducted alongside our United States Air Force partners, enable our crews to maintain and enhance critical search and rescue skills, while strengthening the interoperability that underpins NATO's collective security," he said. Royal Navy Lt. S. Cass, a flight commander assigned to the 814 Naval Air Squadron, agreed, adding that he hopes to continue working with "our friends across the pond" in the years to come. Reinke called the deployment an unqualified success, not necessarily for any single event but for the readiness training they were able to layer into one exercise. "We were able to use legitimate flight training requirements to generate maximum value, ensuring worldwide readiness while working with our international partners," he said. "We also were able to build strong human relationships with the men and women of our partner nations, laying the kind of foundation that makes coalition operations successful." Spotlight: NATO

title: War Department Prepares to Protect Election From Foreign Interference
text: In less than five weeks, Americans will head to the polls for the U.S. midterm elections. Voting Assistance A guidebook sits on a decorated table during the Federal Voting Assistance Program workshop at Peterson Space Force Base, Colo., June 3, 2026. The workshop equipped unit voting assistance officers with the necessary tools and knowledge to help service members and their families successfully navigate the absentee voting process. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.98 MB ) Credit: Air Force Staff Sgt. Jaime Sanchez VIRIN: 260603-X-IL270-8006 Every seat in the U.S. House of Representatives and a third of U.S. Senate seats, some 470 contests in all, will be decided Nov. 3, and the War Department will help ensure foreign actors don't meddle in those elections. "As we approach this election cycle, we must prove that we can and will protect the integrity of our democratic processes from any threat," said Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. "In my role as secretary of war, the Department of War will effectively wield its capabilities to protect and uphold the reliability of America's voting mechanisms against external manipulation and disruption from foreign actors, while maintaining the fundamental freedoms that characterize our country." In a memorandum published yesterday , Hegseth outlined the department's capabilities he activated to ensure the integrity of the upcoming election. U.S. Cyber Command, along with agencies such as the National Security Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, will use their intelligence and cyber capabilities to ensure foreign actors do not interfere with the U.S. democratic process. "U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency are closely partnered to identify and defend against cyber threats to our nation," said Army Gen. Joshua M. Rudd, Cybercom commander and National Security Agency director. "The command and the agency regularly counter actions by malicious foreign cyber actors, including those with the intent to interfere with our democratic process." The secretary also directed the defense intelligence enterprise to collect information on foreign threats to U.S. elections, analyze it and produce useful guidance based on those findings. Finally, he directed Cybercom to work alongside the Department of Homeland Security to counter any potential cyber threats from foreign actors targeting U.S. elections. Election Guide Federal Voting Assistance Program materials are available for service members during a workshop at Joint Base Charleston, S.C., April 1, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 675.84 KB ) Credit: Air Force Airman 1st Class Nahaku Takahashi VIRIN: 260401-F-RS563-1015 "We have very important elections coming up. We want those elections to be honest," President Donald J. Trump told Americans during a July 16 address to the nation. "You can't have a great country without free and fair elections." Hegseth said the War Department would play a critical role in ensuring that happens. "Our nation's ability to conduct free and fair elections is a steadfast principle of our democracy. Assuring and protecting this ability is a no-fail mission and the DOW will do its part in supporting this whole-of-government effort," Hegseth said. "In America, the people rule, and we must ensure that their voice remains sovereign, secure and entirely undiluted." title: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth SpSecretary of War Pete Hegseth Speech on the Arsenal of Freedom in Austin, TX (As Delivered)
text: SECRETARY OF WAR PETE HEGSETH: Thank you, Dino. Thank you for that incredible introduction. I remember that speech. In fact, it was about a year ago, and we pledged to wage a war of attrition against the Pentagon bureaucracy to open our building up to companies just like this one, to fast runners that are ready to run hard, build at scale, take risks, invest, are doing it for the right reasons. We can't just have the big companies at the top doing all the work and not doing it fast enough. We need the best companies in this country, American manufacturing, American made, and that's what you're doing right here at Saronic, right here in Texas for the Arsenal of Freedom tour. It's great to be here with you. Just since we are here in Texas, I want to thank a couple of, they become dear friends and great advocates for your company or your state, but also for what we're doing in our department. Congressman August Pfluger and Morgan Luttrell. I see Morgan right there. Congressman Pfluger and Congressman Luttrell have been not just with me from day one, but with our cause from day one. Backing us up when things were difficult, when things were easy, when they were good, when they were bad, when we were having to tell hard truths. They've had our back. So, gentlemen, thank you very much for everything you do for us. Appreciate it. So we've traveled the country, meeting with great companies and innovators. And one thing is for certain: thanks to President Trump, thanks to the efforts of the Department of War, but more importantly to great Americans like you, American manufacturing is back. American-made is back, and not a minute too soon. And not for show, not for peacetime, but for victory, a lasting victory, one that will secure our freedoms for generations to come. Now, having had a chance to tour this facility firsthand just a few moments ago, the scale, investment, and precision of your projects is truly impressive. You are on the front lines of American industry. And that's the entire purpose of the Arsenal of Freedom tour. I had a chance to shake some hands along the assembly line there, the production line, but the point, as Dino said, of this tour is to look patriots in the eye and thank you for the work that you've done and for the work that you're doing. Every helmet out there slinging lead on our behalf is doing it because of a hard hat enabling them that stands behind them. That's you. That's your mission inside this company with what you're building with these beautiful boats, ships, whatever the navy calls them…vessels, thank you very much, on behalf of our warfighters. But I know, and you especially know more than I do, that the greatness of Saronic was not simply wished into existence. It didn't appear in thin air. What exists between these walls was forged. It was forged by the investment and the labor and the expertise and the sheer willpower of each of you standing here today. In some ways, I would say this a call this a field of dreams company. Remember the phrase: If you build it, they will come. In some ways, that's what Saronic has done. You built it knowing we need it, and we are here because we're going to use it, and we appreciate everything you put into it. You know this here in Texas, but the political swamp creatures in Washington D.C. They see they just don't necessarily understand that mission. They're experts in the art of sitting back, lobbying, collecting a government paycheck, and coasting off the labor of what was built by others. They produce nothing, build nothing, or worse, they outsource it and then block out competitors in our own country. But you are the innovators, the builders of the Arsenal of Freedom. It is precisely the strength of our domestic manufacturing and arsenal and industry that keeps us free. American manufacturing, American made, American jobs, American power. And as Morgan reminded me, nobody does it bigger than Texas. It's a fact. The future of warfare will be built on the backs of AI and autonomy, which is a top priority of this War Department to ensure our warfighters, whether they see less direct conflict or not, and they probably will see less direct conflict because of autonomy, but they'll be more lethal, which is what's even more important. Saronic is the gold standard of what a company should be doing to achieve this. Take, for example, in the past, recovery missions required manned ships to conduct search and rescue in the direct line of adversary fire, like say the Strait of Hormuz. Well, just this last June, 2 U.S. Army AH-64 Apache pilots went down in contested waters near Oman. Saronic’s rapidly fielded, and I can attest it was rapidly fielded. Twenty four-foot autonomous vessel built right here in Austin, the Corsair USV, navigated forward and safely pulled the two pilots out of harm's way, marking the first known combat search and rescue mission executed by an autonomous vessel in American history. You did that. Those pilots are alive today because of the incredible innovation under this very roof. You should be, and rightfully are, incredibly proud of that feat. I just would…I remember that day thinking, "What the faces of those pilots must have looked like? What is this thing? Where are the sailors? Do I trust it? Does it speak to me? I remember thinking the options were the Omani Coast Guard. There were other things, and then an hour later, the report came to me…no, no, no, it was the unmanned surface vessel. I just thought only America. Only our companies, only our innovators, only our workers, and you raced it to the battlefield, and it has had great effect. The Corsair is also proving itself on offense in combat strike operations. In July, CENTCOM, you've seen the video. I've seen it. The world's seen it. Employed the Corsair to strike a submarine and ship maintenance facility at the Bandar Abbas Naval Base in the Persian Gulf. The operation degraded Iran's ability to continue attacking commercial shipping and marked the first operational employment of sea drones in U.S. military combat operations. Now, those are the kind of firsts that we like. What Saronic demonstrates is the future of American naval power, delivering over 300 combat-proven Corsairs, rapidly fielding the 52-foot Mirage, and scaling blue water reach with the 180-foot Marauder, all built in under a year. In our building, we're used to timelines of seven, eight years, one year is not a thing. It's like you're a mirage. But I came to see that it's real. That's the kind of scale and speed that our department needs, the kind of competition our building needs, the bureaucracy needs to realize that it can be done. Because if we go at the pace we've done in the past, we won't have what the warfighters of today and the future actually need. You are no longer testing concepts; you are deploying lethal autonomous mass to ensure our fleet commands the sea. You are the front lines of American power. You see, part of what makes Saronic exceptional is not just the technology; it's the warfighter DNA driven into every line of code and every weld, founded and operated by Veterans like the man who introduced me, Navy SEAL veteran Dino Mavrookas, eight combat tours. Marine veteran Rob Lehman. This team builds with the urgency of those who know firsthand what is at stake. And then partnering directly with our SkillBridge program and our service academies, Serana creates a premier pipeline for military and Veteran talent. Just as critically, you are transitioning skilled civilian American welders and machinists and fabricators from automotive and aerospace industries into cutting-edge naval shipbuilding. All I can say to that is more, please. We, thousands of miles away, are deeply and profoundly grateful for the work that you do, day in and day out. And I'm here on behalf of a president who demands the urgency, innovation, and combat power that this place delivers every single day. A president who has, from his very first day in office, operated on core principles of pure and unadulterated common sense. We put America, American citizens, and America first. The only real path to American security and strength is peace through strength. And a nation that cannot build for itself, a nation that cannot create its own tools, its own defenses, or its own future, is a nation that is in managed decline. And for too long, elites, especially on one side, but in both parties, sat idly by and accepted a backward status quo, but not President Trump. He recognized that decline is indeed a choice, a choice that must be fundamentally rejected in real time. And in doing so, he has unleashed a great American revival, a reawakening of the American industrial spirit and national confidence, as he calls it, rightfully so, a golden age for America that you are all a part of in this building. As his Secretary of War, my mission is to ignite this revival within our armed forces. And since day one, that mission has had three pillars upon which we stand. First, we're reviving the warrior ethos within our fighting force, reminding our warriors that their sole purpose is to be the most lethal fighting force on the planet. Full stop. We're not here to do social engineering, or social justice, or gender bending, or DEI, or dudes and dresses. We're just back to basics. That's what we do at the War Department. Second, we're rebuilding our military. We've seen a historic trillion-dollar investment thus far in the last budget, and you will see even more. And not just in platforms but in people. We're asking for $1.5 trillion in the current budget to make generational investments to keep our country strong and sustain good, high-paying jobs for American manufacturers like Saronic. We will deliver on this generational investment, we will fund this department. The president is committed to it, as are we, as are our partners in Congress, as are these congressmen and their colleagues in the Senate. We will deliver this generational funding and investment, come hell or high water. It just got me thinking. Speaking of hell or high water, those are two things the Iranian Navy are very familiar with at this point. Third, we are reestablishing deterrence. Under the previous administration, the world questioned American strength, and that is no more. The era of doubt and decline is over. Deterrence is back, and the world has taken notice. See, the department we're prudent, but we don't make weapons to store them in piggy banks. We use them to achieve American objectives. Hard power. When narco-terrorists, the Al Qaeda of our hemisphere, when they send drugs to our shores to poison Americans, we no longer catch and release those narco-terrorists. We sink their boats. Deterrence in action. When our southern border was overwhelmed by an illegal invasion, we secured it. Zero crossings, absolute sovereignty, deterrence in action. When American justice was required in Venezuela, hundreds of our best went downtown Caracas, grabbed a dictator, and returned without a single U.S. casualty. Deterrence in action. And when President Trump says that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, he means it. Iran has tried and is trying to blackmail the world with conventional weapons. It's the North Korea approach. So many conventional weapons that they can at their choosing race for a nuclear bomb. Well, under this president, that will never work. The devastation of our military against Iran has been historic. Even if the sheer lies of our so-called media act in service of Iranian state TV. You see, the only media that does fake propaganda better than Iran is our Trump deranged media. I'm serious. It's sad because we've got warriors in harm's way doing incredible things-a difficult, dangerous mission-and we have a deranged media that hate our president more than they love our country. We'll do our job no matter what. We will complete the mission. Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. President Trump holds the cards, deterrence in action. But to win the future as we will, we must build. The Department of War, as Dino mentioned, has been kicking the door wide open for commercial disruptors, non-traditional innovators, and venture-backed builders. We're actively creating the next generation of defense primes, firms like Saronic. Our Arsenal of Freedom tour showcases how modern deterrence requires commercial speed. Our chief technology officer, Emil Michael, who's with us here today, he helped unite our innovation ecosystem under one roof to expedite decisions instead of holding on to legacy bureaucratic delays. When I talk about a war of attrition against the Pentagon bureaucracy, Emil and I and our colleagues stand back to back, machine guns out every single day. And this brings me to my promise and my challenge to every industry leader in this country: the days of rewarding the comfortable old guard for stagnation and failure are over. We are a different department than we were two years ago, night and day. You see, I don't care what name is on the side of a vessel, or a missile, or a ship. I just want the best. And for too long, it was an oligarchy of a few companies that held everybody out. And our job is to rip that building open and allow the competition to be level, so that any great company in America can compete to build that vessel, that missile, or that ship. And the fastest runner will win. And if it's not Saronic, fine. But if it's Saronic, great. Whoever it is, whoever's the best, will win at today's War Department. We're moving from bureaucracy to business. The acquisitions reforms we've made, the emphasis on a modern technology stack, the way we're working with industry, all centered around the capabilities and speed needed for a modern military. We will provide larger, longer, and more predictable contracts to companies like Serrano, companies that can actually deliver at pace and at scale. We will reward leaders who choose to invest in their workers, who expand their capacity, who share in our sense of urgency. That's been one of the biggest things we've had to infuse into the defense industrial base: a sense of urgency. We reward those who choose to deploy their resources toward bolstering production, as you have in multiple facilities, instead of stock buyback programs. The message is simple: If you deliver for America, this Pentagon, this War Department, will have your back. If you do not, we will show you the door. And look at what Saronic is doing for Texas and for Louisiana. In Texas, under the governor's leadership, we are witnessing the rebirth of American maritime power. Since 2022, Saronic has scaled up to over 1,200 Texas employees, operating 540,000 square feet across Austin and conducting cutting-edge maritime trials in Galveston. Saronic's partnership with the department is projected to generate over 260 billion dollars in economic impact for the Lone Star State alone. At the port of Brownsville, Port Alpha, pretty impressive, I must say, delivers a $3 billion investment, up to 10,000 high-paying jobs, over 160 billion in regional impact for Cameron County, and 150,000…this is what I love to hear, gross tons of new shipbuilding capacity. The industrial muscle here will double domestic shipbuilding and ensure absolute dominance. This momentum. It'll also transform Louisiana, and the governor there is restoring working waterfronts. We need to revive and bring back our waterfronts. Through modernizing the historic Gulf craft shipyard in Franklin and establishing a new engineering hub in New Orleans, Saronic is executing a 300 million, 300 plus million investment to build autonomous surface vessels. This effort creates over 1,500 high-paying maritime careers. So together, Franklin and New Orleans prove that combining historic craft with robotics creates an unbeatable industrial edge. You see, in complex theaters like the Pacific, deterrence demands capability, capacity, but also, and most importantly, credibility-a credible capability, a credible threat. Innovation like what is happening at Saronic will allow us to deliver the kind of magazine depth, operational unpredictability, and create targeting dilemmas for adversaries. We are fielding, each and every day, that arsenal of freedom that will be required on that edge. Saronic embodies this sovereign standard on the shop floor. Again, from the edge to the shop floor. That's how I need you, I want you to think about it every single day. That's the essence of the arsenal of freedom. What you do is not just build a widget; you build a sword, a tool, a vessel for a warfighter halfway around the globe who utterly depends on your precision, on your lethality, on what you put in their hands. And the Corsair is manufactured in an important way entirely with American materials and hands sourced through a network of 94 American suppliers across 27-not 27 countries, 27 American states. American-made, American manufacturing, American jobs, American power. Because as you know, our American warriors-they are second to none, the best in the world and the best of our country, the real 1%. You know, in places like Washington D.C., New York City, Austin, they like to talk about the elite, the 1%, the privileged. No, no, no. The real 1% are the ones you serve, are the ones I serve, the men and women who raise the right hand to defend our republic, who put their life on the line in dark, dangerous, difficult places and sign up to defend us, to defend me and defend you. They are the absolute real 1%, the real elite of our nation. But while our warriors are that 1% and the tip of the spear, you are what sharpens them. All the strategies from the Pentagon are meaningless without the people on this floor, the technicians, the machinists, the fabricators, and the engineers. Every platform you weld, wire, and assemble gives our warfighters the decisive edge to win and return home. Never forget that direct line from your hands to the success of our warfighters. So today I say to you, build faster, scale larger, and deliver more. We need you like never before, because when America is unleashed, we win. But I hear that when Texas is unleashed, we dominate. It's incredible to work through a president who has reminded me time and time again to remind the war fighters time and time again that he has their back. It's all-it's the one thing I always wanted to hear when I was a lieutenant, a platoon leader leading men in combat. I needed to know that my commander had my back if I had to make a difficult decision. And so everywhere I go, talking to troops that will have a chance to do that today, and to the corps of cadets at A&M tomorrow, reminding them that we will have their back, that the president has their back that they are unleashed to fight with violence and decisiveness against our enemies, which is what which is what is required in a combat scenario. Just know that while we have their back, you have theirs, and I think there's been no better…and it's good for the media to capture this…there's been no better and clearer direct line from corporate innovation, defense corporate innovation to the front lines than what's happened here at Ceramic. I've just seen it at CENTCOM. You've seen the way they've adapted in a dynamic environment and then put to use new technologies that, under a different Pentagon with a different mindset, may have taken years and years to develop and test and manufacture and QC (quality control). Instead, the idea is let's get this technology rapidly fielded to the front, where, A, we can use it and B, we can test it and then we can iterate on it because we've got members of the company forward with those fighting to get that feedback in real time to improve that product and use it more effectively next time. That is the feedback loop. That is the dynamic at all domains in which America will fight and fight successfully in the future. Whether it's in the Middle East, whether it's in our hemisphere, or whether it's in the Pacific, it will be real-time innovation with our best innovators and our best war fighters, out-innovating, out-scaling, out-competing our adversaries who just can't do what you do. They may try to copy it, or steal it, or replicate it in some way, but they can't do precisely what you do, and that is a decisive advantage for us. So, as I said, keep going. We see it, and we appreciate it every single day. God bless this great country, and God bless the Republic of Texas as well. Thank you.

title: Meritocracy at Center of Military Service, Hegseth Tells Cadets at Texas A&M
text: At Texas A&M University in College Station, Texas, today, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth told future officers that the U.S. military they will enter places a premium on meritocracy, and that once they put on their uniforms, they will march into formations that value them only for what they bring to the fight. 23:05 "Under the leadership of our commander in chief, President Donald J. Trump, our doctrine is clear: America first and peace through strength," Hegseth said. "And we achieve it in three distinct ways: reviving the warrior ethos, rebuilding our military and reestablishing deterrence here at home and across the globe." The secretary said that he knew restoring the warrior ethos also meant establishing a military centered on meritocracy rather than non-merit factors. "Two days after taking office, I signed the memorandum restoring America's fighting force," he said. "That directive established a bedrock standard that will guide your entire military service ... the armed forces of the United States will be governed strictly by merit, competence and combat readiness." The War Department, he said, is colorblind, gender-neutral and merit-based. "The only thing that matters are our standards, discipline, readiness, training and lethality," he said. "And we will never compromise on those standards." Walking onto the campus this morning, Hegseth said he was impressed by what he saw. "I do not see an academic institution trying to apologize for American strength; I see backbone and resolve, and the uncompromising future of the United States and the United States armed forces," he said. "I see a real, grounded, strong institution, which is exactly what our nation needs." The secretary's visit to Texas A&M University was part of a two-day trip. Yesterday, he visited Saronic, a defense contractor that builds autonomous ocean-going drones — one of which was used to rescue two AH-64 Apache pilots off the coast of Oman. Later that day, he administered the oath of enlistment to dozens of recruits, and today, he administered the oath of office to ROTC cadets. The secretary said what he sees in Texas is the entire package of what's needed to rebuild the U.S. military. "Just down the road, innovators are forging unmanned vessels, autonomous systems, drones, hypersonic missiles that will define modern deterrence," Hegseth said. "But standing right here in College Station, I'm looking at the indispensable other half of that equation: the future warfighters. ... The arsenal of freedom builds the sword right here in Texas, but that blade will be wielded as it always has been, by the Aggies standing in front of me today." The secretary reminded cadets that during World War II, more than 20,000 Aggies served, and that their school provided more leaders to the U.S. military than any other source outside the U.S. service academies. The same remains true today, he said. Not all of the men and women in the Texas A&M Corps of Cadets will go on to join the U.S. military — about 40% eventually accept a commission to serve. But those who do choose to serve, Hegseth said, will become part of the proud military history of the school. For those men and women, he said, he promised to always give them what they need so they can be best equipped to serve as they have sworn to do. "I make you this personal pledge: just as my fellow soldiers had my back on the battlefield in Iraq and Afghanistan, I will always have your back," he said. "And you can know that our commander in chief has your back every single day." Hegseth said his job at the Pentagon is to get them the weaponry, training, technology, and mission clarity they need to fight, win and then get home. He promised to do that. "We will never tie your hands behind your back; silly rules of engagement are gone. Warfighters are unleashed, and we [will] never ask you to apologize for being warriors," he said. "We will demand excellence, and at the same time, back you to the hilt. So, train hard, demand more of yourselves than anyone else would ever dare demand of you, uphold the honor of that uniform ... honor the memory of the Aggies who marched before you ... [and] prepare to lead the most formidable fighting force the world has ever known." Spotlight: Value of Service News: Hegseth Addresses Team Who Built Sea Drone Used to Rescue Downed Apache Crew Experience: Delivering Peace Through Strength News: 'We've Got Their Back,' Hegseth Tells Parents of Enlistees in Texas

title: Joint Task Force Southern Border Soldiers Innovate to Reinforce Barriers
text: Border Barrier Soldiers assigned to Joint Task Force Southern Border, supporting Operation Ardent Vanguard, place concertina wire on top of Hesco barriers at National Defense Area 2 near Fort Hancock, Texas, Aug. 6, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 3.99 MB ) Credit: Army Spc. Sean Hoch VIRIN: 260806-A-MA561-9014 Soldiers with the 62nd Engineer Battalion, 36th Engineer Brigade, assigned to Joint Task Force Southern Border in support of Operation Ardent Vanguard, recently reinforced a challenging section of the southern border barrier. The soldiers emplaced two strands of concertina wire and one strand of razor wire atop 7-foot Hesco barriers in National Defense Area 2 near Fort Hancock, Texas. The reinforced barriers disrupt climbing attempts and enhance persistent detection, monitoring and rapid response along high-risk border corridors. "Barrier reinforcement operations represent more than physical infrastructure; they showcase the technical ingenuity and skill of our service members," said Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, commander of Joint Task Force Southern Border and the 1st Armored Division and Fort Bliss, Texas. "For the last 14 weeks, our great soldiers have been out here day and night developing innovative solutions to stop human trafficking in our own territory." In May, the Navy and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began installing 10 miles of barriers under orders from the War Department and U.S. Northern Command. Within about 30 days, they constructed 10 miles of barriers, including site preparation, mobilization, environmental clearance, receiving barrier sections from overseas, and transporting more than 90,000 cubic yards of fill material. On average, constructing 10 miles of Hesco barriers takes approximately 28 days when crews work 12-hour shifts. However, this timeline does not include mobilization, land clearing or compaction. During the recent reinforcement operation, soldiers assigned to the 591st Combat Engineer Company-Infantry, 62nd Engineer Battalion, maintained a demanding pace as they reinforced barriers from Santa Teresa, New Mexico, to Fort Hancock, Texas. "When we work on border reinforcement operations, we typically start in the morning, and then we work until around midafternoon," said Army 2nd Lt. Jonah Posada, a Sapper platoon leader with the 591st. "And then, we'll return to Fort Bliss and prepare for the next day; we try to continue at that pace for the whole week." To address site conditions and avoid the Texas summer heat, the company adopted an offset work schedule: one platoon began work in the early evening; another relieved it and worked until late morning. The elevated work surface and limited workspace made installing razor wire on the Hesco barriers difficult. Additionally, the soldiers could not use metal stakes, which are generally used for support, because they would place compressive stress on the barriers. Instead, they used boom lifts as work platforms to emplace razor wire atop the concertina wire. The final 300-meter section presented another significant challenge: soft, uneven terrain prevented the boom lifts from reaching the area and attempts to move the equipment left them stuck. Rather than leave the section unfinished, the 591st soldiers developed a solution using equipment already available. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} "We devised a plan using tent poles and rope that we had in our high-angle mountaineering kit," Posada said. "Using those ropes, we stretched [the section of wire] out and kept tension on the razor wire." Soldiers on the ground used camouflage-net poles to lift the razor wire while teams atop the barrier secured it in place. A carabiner attached to a rope helped lift the wire from the ground, enabling the soldiers to complete the final section without relying on boom lifts. The solution was the latest in a series of adaptations soldiers developed as they transitioned between traditional barrier work and reinforcing Hesco barriers. The Hesco barriers introduced additional challenges because the razor wire configuration was not standard for the engineers. "The actual obstacle that we emplaced on top of the Hesco [barriers] is not normal," Posada said. "We had to figure out how to best overcome that. The terrain by the Hesco was a big hindrance on the mission as well." The company also developed techniques to prevent injuries. In one method, the soldiers attached a wooden post to a boom lift and used it to position the wire across the barrier. The completed work reinforces the barrier with additional obstacles intended to deter unauthorized crossings and support the broader border-security mission. Posada said the U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents appreciated the efforts and noted that the additional barriers helped limit crossings. The operation underscores the role of combat engineers in providing practical solutions when terrain, equipment and mission requirements intersect. For the soldiers conducting the work, the operation demonstrated the importance of adapting established engineering practices to conditions on the ground. Posada said he shared the techniques that his platoon developed with other platoon leaders in the company so they could apply the lessons learned to similar missions. Spotlight: DOW Support to the Southern Border

title: NORAD F-16s Deploy to High North Under Operation Arctic Vanguard
text: Arctic Formation U.S. Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft and a KC-135 Stratotanker fly in formation while conducting aerial refueling as part of Operation Arctic Vanguard over Greenland, Sept. 16, 2026. The operation is a joint and multinational effort designed to enhance interoperability, test cold-weather combat readiness and strengthen coalition capabilities across the Arctic. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 2.05 MB ) Credit: Air Force Maj. David Brown VIRIN: 260916-D-D0962-9549 The Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region deployed F-16 Fighting Falcons from Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, to Goose Bay, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, in support of Operation Arctic Vanguard 26-4.2. During this NORAD operation, Alaskan NORAD Region is operating directly alongside the Canadian NORAD Region to execute critical defense missions across the Arctic, Sept. 13-26. Under Arctic Vanguard, NORAD personnel and aircraft will forward deploy into Greenland to execute operations in austere conditions alongside partners from Denmark and other NATO countries. This operation supports the NORAD and U.S. Northern Command Nordic Bridge concept, which aligns the commands' Arctic operations, exercises and training, activities and investments with other U.S. combatant commands, NATO, individual nations and regional partners. "Operation Arctic Vanguard demonstrates that austere conditions and vast distances present no barrier to NORAD's collective defense," said Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert D. Davis, commander, Alaskan NORAD Region. "Deploying combat airpower from Alaska across Canada and forward into Greenland validates our agile combat capabilities and demonstrates our seamless integration with the Canadian NORAD region, the Kingdom of Denmark and our NATO allies. Together, we maintain continuous vigilance and credible deterrence across North America's northern approaches." {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} Operation Arctic Vanguard is part of a recurring series of NORAD and Northcom operations conducted across the North American Arctic region to enhance presence, operate from forward Arctic locations and defend North America's northern approaches. Under the Nordic Bridge concept and efforts to bring orchestration to operations, activities and investments in the Arctic, Operation Arctic Vanguard enables more consistent presence of multinational forces in the region, operating in multiple domains and in varying locations. title: DOW Hosts 2nd Interagency Summit to Strengthen Counter-Drone Defense
text: Joint Interagency Task Force 401 hosted its second interagency summit last month to accelerate cooperation against rapidly evolving drone threats. Drone Summit Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, Joint Interagency Task Force 401 director, speaks at an interagency summit in Alexandria, Va., Aug. 21, 2026. Hosted by JIATF 401, the summit accelerated whole-of-government cooperation against the rapidly evolving threat of unmanned aircraft systems. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 471.04 KB ) Credit: Army Lt. Col. Adam Scher VIRIN: 260821-A-MJ360-9316 The gathering brought together more than 200 leaders and experts from 75 departments and agencies to synchronize efforts to strengthen homeland defense against drones. The task force is the War Department's premier counter-unmanned aircraft agency. Building on the momentum following the first full year since it was established in August 2025, the summit emphasized growing interagency partnerships that are rapidly delivering counter-UAS capabilities to warfighters, federal partners and local law enforcement. "Drones have fundamentally changed the operational environment," said Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, JIATF 401 director. "To meet this challenge, we must outpace our adversaries by working together to deliver capabilities quickly. This summit is one way we are synchronizing a whole-of-government effort to secure our borders, defend the national airspace and protect the American people." Discussions primarily focused on establishing a unified, cross-domain common operating picture for air traffic in areas critical for national security. Participants also took part in collaborative breakout groups focused on five key areas of counter-UAS integration for homeland defense: Major-event and critical-infrastructure preparation; Reporting, jurisdiction and information sharing; Authorities, policy and legislation; Capability access and the counter-UAS marketplace; Testing, standards and integration. The summit allowed participants to identify challenges, share best practices and strengthen coordination across agencies, while also highlighting innovations in the counter-UAS marketplace pioneered by JIATF 401. Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems Summit From left, retired Air Force Gen. Glen D. Vanherck, former commander of U.S. Northern Command and North American Aerospace Defense Command; Jarred Conley, Defense Innovation Unit portfolio director; and Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, Joint Interagency Task Force 401 director, participate in a panel during a counter-unmanned aircraft systems summit at National Harbor, Md., Aug. 25, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 235.52 KB ) Credit: Army Lt. Col. Adam Scher VIRIN: 260825-A-MJ360-9247 It also highlighted the War Department's efforts to transition emerging counter-UAS technologies from testing toward operational employment. The task force is conducting a directed-energy pilot program at multiple military installations to evaluate high-energy lasers, high-power microwaves and other novel technologies in an operational environment. Together, these initiatives demonstrate JIATF 401's commitment to accelerating innovation, strengthening interagency partnerships and delivering effective counter-drone capabilities to the warfighter. "My charge for this summit is for each of you to walk away with specific actions to address problems," Ross said. "We are all in this together, and it will take all of us working together to effectively counter the threat of drones and keep our warfighters and the American people safe." The summit concluded with a unified commitment to maintain continuous interagency teamwork and information sharing. By aligning efforts across the department, interagency partners and federal agencies, JIATF 401 continues to cut through bureaucracy and rapidly deliver state-of-the-art counter-drone capabilities to warfighters worldwide. title: Southern Vanguard 2026 Turns Peruvian Jungle Into a Classroom
text: Wet Work U.S. soldiers assigned to the 551st Infantry Regiment perform jungle waterborne training during Exercise Southern Vanguard 26 in Sauce, Peru, Sept. 9, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 5.61 MB ) Credit: Army Sgt. Grace Wajler VIRIN: 260909-Z-DX231-9035 Movement slows. Equipment gets heavier. Water becomes an obstacle instead of a landmark. The environment quietly strips away assumptions about how quickly a formation should move or how easily a soldier can accomplish a familiar task. For U.S. soldiers training alongside Peruvian and Chilean forces during Exercise Southern Vanguard 26, that friction is exactly the point. In the hills surrounding Sauce, Peru, soldiers are learning to move, survive and operate in terrain where their Peruvian counterparts have spent years developing expertise. During the opening days of jungle warfare training, multinational formations started at various lanes, including amphibious movement, survival skills and small-unit tactics designed for an environment that can punish even routine movement. Jungle Portrait Army Capt. Jared Fonzi, an operations planner assigned to the 551st Infantry Regiment, U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, joins approximately 400 warfighters to execute Exercise Southern Vanguard 26 in Peru, Sept. 10, 2026. The field training and command post exercise takes place in a demanding, austere jungle environment and includes combined operations designed to simulate real-world contingencies in the complex terrain of the jungle hills of the Amazon. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 5.33 MB ) Credit: Army Staff Sgt. Mickey Miller VIRIN: 260910-Z-HY815-9036 "Multiply fatigue by 10," Army Capt. Jared Fonzi, an operations planner assigned to the 551st Infantry Regiment, U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, said while describing the physical effects of jungle operations. "The climate, the terrain, the physical exhaustion that everyone here goes through — pictures do not justify the stress and the physical fatigue." Southern Vanguard 26 is a multinational exercise hosted by the Peruvian Army and designed to strengthen interoperability among participating forces while building proficiency in jungle mobility, survivability and tactical operations. For American soldiers, participation offers something difficult to replicate at home: The opportunity to become students of a partner force operating in a terrain it understands intimately. Fonzi, a graduate of the Jungle Operations Training Course-Panama, Ranger School and an infantry officer proficient with conventional U.S. tactics, said jungle warfare changes the scale at which soldiers must think and maneuver. "The size of the maneuvering element is far smaller," he said. "You don't really maneuver as a platoon, which is usually the bread and butter of U.S. operations. Here, with smaller elements — team size, squad size — you need to rely more on individual survival techniques and minimal equipment." That emphasis places greater importance on survival, fieldcraft and understanding the environment itself. Humidity, elevation, water obstacles, rainfall and dense vegetation are not simply background conditions. "These climate differences and natural elements are what affect the fight," Fonzi said. That reality is also driving U.S. soldiers to look outward for expertise. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} Fonzi said U.S. forces are relying heavily on jungle warfare specialists from countries such as Peru, Colombia and Panama to understand how forces accustomed to the environment operate and which techniques might improve U.S. tactics, techniques and procedures. The dynamic is visible throughout Southern Vanguard 26. Peruvian instructors are leading much of the jungle training, while U.S. instructors work alongside them and help translate techniques for American formations. Fonzi described the Peruvian approach as aggressive and immediate, often moving soldiers quickly from instruction into practical application. "There's really no crawl phase here," he said. "They'll give a brief instruction, and then they just throw them in the water or whatever training environment they go into." The approach may differ from how many American soldiers are accustomed to training, but adapting to unfamiliar methods is part of the exercise itself. Interoperability is often discussed in terms of radios, procedures and whether two formations can communicate on a battlefield. But before any of that works, soldiers have to understand how their partners think, move and solve problems. Sometimes that begins with something as unremarkable as getting everyone across a body of water. That process requires a certain humility. The U.S. military brings considerable capability nearly anywhere it goes. The jungle offers a useful reminder that capability and expertise are not the same thing. Sometimes readiness means arriving prepared to teach. Other times, it means recognizing when someone else has something to teach you. Southern Vanguard creates room for both. For soldiers operating beneath the jungle canopy, the lessons are as physical as they are tactical. "Being wet 24/7, fighting through brush, crossing water — these little things have a huge impact on how you fight," Fonzi said. Over the course of the exercise, those small hardships become part of a larger test: whether multinational formations can adapt together in an environment that does not care how experienced, capable or well-equipped they were before entering it. That may ultimately be the most valuable lesson hidden beneath the canopy. Partnerships become meaningful when soldiers learn to depend on one another before circumstances require them to.

title: USS St. Louis Assumes U.S. Northern Command Mission at Southern Border
text: Maritime Security The littoral combat ship USS St. Louis departs Naval Station Mayport, Fla., in support of U.S. Northern Command's mission to secure the southern border of the United States, Sept. 13, 2026. Littoral combat ships are fast, agile, mission-focused platforms designed to operate in near-shore environments and defeat 21st century coastal threats, supporting the Navy's goals of forward presence, maritime security, sea control and deterrence. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.98 MB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 1st Class Keenan Daniels VIRIN: 260913-N-VW723-1260 The littoral combat ship USS St. Louis departed Naval Station Mayport, Florida, in support of U.S. Northern Command's mission to secure the southern border of the United States, Sept. 13. The St. Louis assumes duties previously executed by the USS Cooperstown in support of Northcom's border security objectives. The command is working together with the Department of Homeland Security to augment U.S. Customs and Border Protection along the southern border to disrupt illicit drug trafficking and protect the homeland. "Our crew has trained relentlessly for this deployment, and they stand ready for whatever challenges lie ahead. I could not be more proud to lead these sailors," said Navy Cmdr. Lester Shewmake, commanding officer of the USS St. Louis. "To our families and the Mayport community — thank you for your unwavering support as we head to sea." Navy assets are deployed under Northcom's maritime homeland defense authorities to enable maritime interdiction missions to prevent the flow of illegal drugs or other illegal activity. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} The St. Louis is assigned to the Littoral Combat Ship Squadron 2 and homeported in Mayport. It is a class of small surface combatants armed with capabilities to defeat challenges in the world's littorals. These ships can operate independently or in high-threat scenarios as part of a networked battle force that includes larger, multimission surface combatants such as cruisers and destroyers. It is the 22nd littoral combat ship delivered to the Navy, the 10th Freedom-variant to join the fleet and the seventh ship to bear the name. The first St. Louis, a sloop of war, was launched in 1828.
