title: Hegseth, German Counterpart Agree to Advance Defense Industrial Cooperation
text: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Boris Pistorius, Germany's defense minister, met today at the Pentagon to discuss NATO 3.0, increased European defense spending and the defense industrial bases of both nations. "We're here to take another strong step in advancing our defense industrial cooperation between the United States and Germany," Hegseth said. Nato Partners The German, American and POW/MIA flags fly above Katterbach Army Airfield as U.S. Army AH-64E Apache helicopters fly in formation in Bavaria, Germany, Feb. 2, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.81 MB ) Credit: Army Spc. Grant Hockley VIRIN: 171230-A-GH759-4703 Last year at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Hegseth said allied nations must spend more on defense; President Donald J. Trump set the bar at 5% of gross domestic product. He added that increases in troop readiness, weapons production and force contributions were also needed. Hegseth, who calls the proposed changes NATO 3.0, said Germany has been "front and center" in making them happen. "Today, we see major progress that no one would have thought possible," he said. "Germany today is moving closer to fulfilling the 5% — leading the way on the spending commitment it made at the Hague Summit last year — but as we talked about, defense spending is just the first step." The secretary noted that increasing defense production on both sides of the Atlantic is essential. "NATO 3.0 will also require putting Germany's very large and historic industrial base to work for the common defense," Hegseth said. "It's the same thing that we're doing right here, as I and members of our team travel across the country; as we rebuild our arsenal of freedom." The arsenal of freedom plan, Hegseth said, aims to reindustrialize the U.S., rebuild American manufacturing, manufacture American-made products and create American jobs. The two civilian military leaders signed an agreement that, Hegseth said, aligns the War Department's acquisition transformation strategy with Germany's Procurement Acceleration Act. "When we align the two, you expand opportunities for joint development, production, licensed manufacturing, and expanded maintenance and sustainment capacities — exactly what allied countries should be doing," he said. "The objective is straightforward: Deliver capable systems to American, German and allied forces, at scale and at speed for maximum lethality." Pistorius highlighted Germany's immense increase in defense spending and said it's on board with the NATO 3.0 vision and with balancing out the burden of defending the NATO alliance. "Germany is strengthening its defense capabilities and acts as a driving force in Europe," he said. "We Europeans want to take some of the burden off the U.S. and assume primary responsibility for conventional deterrence in Europe." The German defense minister noted that since last year, Germany has increased defense spending by 25%, equivalent to about $147 billion. "We are investing in new state-of-the-art weapon systems here in the U.S.; we are assuming a leading role within NATO and, when it comes to providing support to Ukraine, we are strengthening NATO's eastern flank, particularly through our armored brigade in Lithuania," he said. He also highlighted German investments in technology, including space and deep-precision strike capabilities. Later this week, Germany will also roll out its first F-35A aircraft. The U.S.-Germany agreement, he said, will help Germany become an even stronger NATO partner than it has been for more than 70 years. "It creates a strong basis for closer armament cooperation between our two nations with one clear aim: increasing our production capacity," Pistorius said. He added that the NATO alliance must feature stronger European leadership to survive, and Germany will play a big part in that. "NATO needs to become more European in order to stay transatlantic," he said. "Burden shifting is progressing. Together with our allies, we are working towards a stronger Europe and a stronger NATO. And together with our American friends, we are working on strengthening our common defense and resilience." Spotlight: Acquisition Transformation Spotlight: NATO

title: Department of War Announces a $450 Million Investment in The Elmet Group to Secure America's Tungsten Supply Chain
text: The Department of War's Office of the Assistant Secretary of War for Industrial Base Policy, in partnership with the Economic Defense Unit, announced today a $450 million redeemable preferred equity investment in The Elmet Group through the Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program. This strategic investment will strengthen domestic tungsten capacity, bolster U.S. industrial resilience and military readiness, and help secure an essential material for the defense industrial base. "This investment reflects the Department's commitment to rebuilding critical industrial capacity in the United States," said assistant secretary of War for industrial base policy Hon. Mike Cadenazzi. "Expanding domestic tungsten processing will strengthen supply chain resilience, support high-quality manufacturing jobs, and reinforce the production base behind essential defense systems." The Elmet Group is the only U.S.-owned, fully integrated producer of tungsten and molybdenum materials and components, supports more than 100 Department of War programs, including the F-35, Patriot PAC-3, Trident D5, NGI, PrSM, and Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines. Tungsten is a foundational input for the defense industrial base, prized for its hardness, heat resistance, density, and durability, and used in critical components across missiles, munitions, aerospace, propulsion, naval, undersea, electronics, and industrial manufacturing applications. "The Economic Defense Unit was created to identify critical industrial chokepoints before adversaries can exploit them and before they become battlefield risk," said George K. Kollitides II, director of the Economic Defense Unit. "Tungsten is essential to the systems that protect American warfighters and sustain deterrence, and this investment helps secure a domestic processing capability the United States cannot afford to leave exposed. By pairing targeted Department support with a disciplined preferred equity structure, we are strengthening the supply chain behind more than 100 defense programs while protecting taxpayers and delivering for the joint force." The Department's investment into Elmet will also establish the only independent ammonium paratungstate facility in North America, which is a key step for tungsten processing and one of the largest chokepoints across the U.S. industrial base. By expanding U.S.-aligned refining and processing capacity, this investment will help reduce reliance on adversary-dominated supply chains in markets where China currently dominates global supply, including an estimated 85 percent of tungsten and 40 percent of molybdenum. The Department's investment is expected to generate substantial economic benefits, including new high-tech jobs across Coldwater, Michigan, and Lewiston, Maine, preserving high-paying manufacturing jobs in Euclid, Ohio, and increasing demand for upstream mining jobs in Nevada. It is also expected to support approximately 1,200 downstream jobs across manufacturing, engineering, and logistics networks tied to major defense suppliers. The investment reflects the Department's broader strategy to secure critical industrial inputs, protect the defense supply chain, and ensure the United States can produce the materials required for sustained military advantage.

title: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth Speech on the Arsenal of Freedom in Oshkosh, WI
text: SECRETARY OF WAR PETE HEGSETH: How are we doing, Oshkosh? [Cheering] John, thank you very much for that gracious introduction and for everything that you do. And thank you all for being here. We're trying to be ahead of schedule for you here, not keep you waiting too long. I just had to go one extra lap on your training course on one of these beauties. They let me drive; it was nice. So, forgive me for being a little late. But I also want to thank our good friend here, a true ally of our warriors in Congress, Congressman Glenn Grothman. Glenn, where are you at? Glenn, thank you. Thank you. [Applause] President Trump talks a lot about 3 a.m. members of Congress, they call at 3 a.m. with extra demands before a key vote. Glenn is not a 3 a.m. guy; he's a reliable vote no matter what. Meaning when you need his vote, he's there to do the right thing on behalf of America First. Congressman, thank you very much. [Applause] Wisconsin's got a great delegation. I also want to thank a true warrior and a true patriot of the highest order, a friend of mine, Congressman Derrick Van Orden. He couldn't be here today, but he's a great advocate for what we stand for, as well as our good friend, Senator Ron Johnson, who runs the Senate Budget Committee; and I know is dedicated to ensuring in the coming weeks and months that the $350 billion reconciliation bill that's going to help fund our $1.5 trillion budget passes. So, Ron Johnson is a great ally, and we appreciate his support. I also want to thank a proud Wisconsinite, Undersecretary of War for Acquisitions and Sustainment, Mike Duffy. Mike, raise your hand. [Applause] Acquisitions and sustainment is like a mouthful of a title, but think of it this way, he is the War Department's official weapons buyer. He's the world's largest arms dealer and his name is Mike Duffy, Department of War. It is a great — great to be here with my team at Oshkosh in the great state of Wisconsin, home to 30,000 defense industrial base workers and 14,000 US service members. And I'm here on behalf of the commander-in-chief, Donald Trump, to say thank you for building faster and faster each day, the Arsenal of Freedom that our warriors need. I'm also here because I want an opportunity to look all of you in the eye, my fellow patriots, and tell you how important your job is. We don't have the helmets without the hard hats, and we don't have the warriors without the workers. We are all shoulder to shoulder in this Arsenal of Freedom. The vehicles you make here, as you know, are used by our warriors all around the world. Every single one of you, every welder, every receptionist to the CEO is supporting American warriors every single day. This is not just another manufacturing job; this is patriotism in the form of steel, past and present. It's incredible what you've accomplished here in Oshkosh. This company has played a role in every major conflict of the last 80 years since World War II. And I've seen your incredible work firsthand downrange, and I know that it saves American lives, the lives of American warriors. Many moons ago, I was a platoon leader in Iraq, fighting an enemy, a cowardly enemy that fought amongst women and children and hid IEDs with stand-off because they knew they couldn't fight American warriors toe to toe. And then Secretary of Defense Robert Gates, after my time in Iraq, but I went back a couple of times as an embedded reporter to see what the troops were up against during the Iraq surge. Robert Gates saw that they needed stronger, safer vehicles to protect our warriors. He cut the usual Pentagon red tape to get Oshkosh MRAPs to our warriors in theater. You and this company saved American lives. There are many American warriors — in fact, I have no doubt many veterans right here today living because of the good work of Midwest manufacturers like you. Their kids, someday their grandkids and their families, thank God, literally, for your work. It's a great American story that we are iterating on and replicating across our Department right now, and I'll explain more about that in a moment. But first, I think what's really special about Oshkosh is that 90 percent of your work is for commercial civilian use. It's great to see integrated production lines of both commercial and defense capabilities. At President Trump's Pentagon, unlike previous Pentagons, unlike what Joe Biden did at Obama did, commercial products and offerings are the default policy. We need more commercial companies in the Department of War space. We are open for business for the best American manufacturers, for all manufacturers. And you no longer have to sue your way into the Department in order to compete. Our job is to make it easier for the big guys and the little guys to get in to compete and ensure that American warriors have the best. You see, we came to Oshkosh because Oshkosh is a model for other commercial manufacturers to step up when your country needs you. From building the beautiful fire trucks I had a chance to see to the family of medium tactical vehicles; you are a model of delivering commercial and military capabilities to the warfighter. Most companies have been in the past too afraid, and rightfully so, of the maze of Pentagon bureaucracy. But I'm here to say we're a different kind of Department, moving at the speed of business, moving at the speed of markets, and we are open for business. We need more Oshkosh across America. During President Trump's first term in office, he rebuilt our military. Now, in his second term, he is rebuilding it yet again. A key piece of legislation passed by this Administration and championed by your representatives, the One Big, Beautiful Bill, specifically secured $190 million in defense contracts executed right here in Wisconsin. And we intend to do more as we move forward, modernizing our forces. This year's defense budget request includes $16.8 billion to modernize Army and Marine Corps combat equipment, which will include the procurement of new futuristic vehicles like the incredible Oshkosh Rogue Fires System. Just two months ago, the United States Marine Corps awarded Oshkosh a well-deserved $92 million contract for the rogue fires system. President Trump has promised a Golden Age of America, and he is delivering all across the country with American manufacturing and rebuilding our Defense Industrial Base. It's a part of the Trump economy that is booming, and that equates to jobs right here in your state and all across America. But I should note, selfishly, since at the War Department, we look at the metrics of our own people as well, that that also includes our military. Under the last Administration, military recruiting was at record lows. You see, they would miss a recruiting number so they would lower the goals and then they would miss that goal. And they would lower it so low that they could barely make it and then say they met their goal. But since November 2024, and something particular happened in November 2024, the U.S. military has seen its highest recruiting records in 30 years. Army, Air Force, Marine Corps, Navy, Space Force, you name it — and they're not just meeting goals, but we're exceeding them months and months in advance. And now with this $1.5 trillion bill, we're going to grow the size of each of those Services, and we're confident we'll meet those new goals as well. So, for the men and women looking to put on camouflage, the Department of War is open for business as well. And what a reflection of confidence from the American people, fathers and mothers to send their sons and daughters in record numbers to go serve. We're humbled by it and honored by it, and we'll continue to do right by them. And part of doing right by them is being right here with you. It's why building our Defense Industrial Base is part of our national defense strategy. It's why burden sharing is so fundamental to who we are and what we do. Every part of what we've focused on has been unleashing American business because we need the best weapons in the hands of warfighters. Right now, there are at least hundreds of thousands of jobs open in America's Defense Industrial Base, including jobs right here in Oshkosh. It was mentioned to me that there's a disproportionate number of vets that work here at this location and across Oshkosh. If you would, please raise your hand if you've served our country in uniform as well. God bless you. [Applause] Thank you. You guys and gals are serving again; it's an extension of service, just like everyone else next to you. You see, this administration knows that Midwest manufacturing doesn't just build our trucks or tanks or airplanes. American manufacturing built the middle class of the Midwest. American made, American manufacturing, American muscle, American money — funding it and in your pockets American jobs. Companies like Oshkosh combine American ingenuity with American work ethic, sheer American work ethic in support of our American warriors. It's an unbeatable combination that none of our adversaries can conceivably match. Well, that speed — I mentioned, Secretary Bob Gates, that was used for the MRAP program, is now what we are demanding for absolutely everything across the War Department. It is the norm, not the exception. We are cutting the red tape to get weapons to warriors in record time. You see, we're not just fighting adversaries. One of my jobs every single day is to go to war with the Pentagon bureaucracy. It is a war of attrition that we intend — our office intends to win. All four years we're going to cut red tape and requirements and ridiculous layers that have been added time and time again, year after year, mostly by lawyers of big companies that want to prevent competition. And we have to tear those barriers down to allow the best companies, America defense or commercial, large or small, to run as fast as possible. That's why we want all of our defense contractors to pivot and that's why we're doing this Arsenal of Freedom, to pivot to a wartime footing and build for victory. As I mentioned, for decades, the Pentagon was hampered by bureaucracy, bogged down by burdensome and inefficient processes, paralyzed by impossible risk thresholds, and distracted by agendas that had nothing to do with war fighting. It was mostly our fault; the world's largest bureaucracy, the Pentagon, sent contractors unstable demand signals. That's part of what we talked about on the factory floor today. Uncertain projections that made the defense industrial base risk averse, slow, lethargic, just like government. The companies that served government started looking like government, falling behind on budget, everything costing more. Ever changing an insane requirement, scheduling overruns became the norm, fat, lazy and complacent companies. Well, those days are over. Speed to delivery is now our organizing principle. We have slashed the culture of bureaucracy, ended the culture of risk aversion, and accelerating a culture of agility, innovation and sheer results. Process is not a result; all that matters is end state and results. No excuses; speed, scale, volume, efficiency, maximum urgency. Every dollar squandered on redundancy or bureaucracy or waste, it's an insult to you, the taxpayer and it's a theft from warfighters. This is a new Department with a new focus on our core mission, where we're restoring the warrior ethos. And that means a focus — an unrelenting, uncompromising focus on lethality. It means no more DEI. It means no more trannies, just training. It means colorblind, gender neutral, merit-based, back to basics across the board no matter if you're carrying a rifle or you're working on the plant floor. President Trump, in fact, he said when he gave me this job — moments afterwards, he said, Pete, I want you to bring the warriors back. [Laughter] Bring them back, and that's what we've done. That's been our focus — uncompromising, without apology from day one. And that's what the Arsenal of Freedom's been all about, bring American manufacturing and jobs and agility back. And that focus on lethality is reestablishing deterrence. We want a military so strong and powerful that our enemies never think about testing us. But as you know, our adversaries are not sitting idly by, they're moving fast. They're developing and delivering new capabilities at a rate that should be sobering for every single American. Which is why President Trump is asking our friends in Congress to pass a $1.5 trillion budget for our warriors. It is a bold, generational investment, the largest military budget in history but it's absolutely necessary. When you look under the hood and you understand the nature of the threat, you understand the negligence of previous Administrations, the deferred maintenance, it is what we must provide for the necessity of today's warriors and in order to make an investment in the future of warfare. Think autonomy and drones, AI, compute space, subsea, hyper sonics, cyber, you name it, we are laying the foundation for continued American dominance here at home, in our hemisphere and around the globe for decades to come, we will build the Arsenal of Freedom. And in the coming months, we will ensure that all of that $1.5 trillion is funded so that our department, working with great companies like this one, can provide it, and working with members of Congress who are willing to give us all the authorities. We need to give companies like Oshkosh stable, clear and consistent demand signals so that you can plan ahead, make more investments, and create more American jobs. I'll say it once and I'll say it again — no more offshoring, outsourcing — American made, American manufacturing, American muscle, American jobs. So, keep doing your part right here on the factory floor. We'll do our part at the Pentagon to keep cutting red tape, allowing you to run as fast as possible and speeding up the procurement process. And, you know, we all know, all of our warriors do their part every single day and every single night all around the world to keep us safe and they remain in our prayers constantly. So, thank you for delivering when it counted and continuing to deliver when it counts. Each one of you ought be proud, and your families, of what you do. Companies like this one are the backbone of the Arsenal of Freedom. Together we're going to guarantee peace through strength for generations to come, which is the point. So, God bless all of your families; God bless our warriors and our great republic. Thank you very much. [Applause]

title: Trump, Hegseth Commemorate 25th Anniversary of 9/11 at the Pentagon
text: President Donald J. Trump, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and other distinguished attendees commemorated the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on U.S. soil during a formal ceremony today in the Pentagon's courtyard. The two leaders were joined by First Lady Melania Trump; Air Force Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; and Condoleezza Rice, who served as secretary of state during 9/11. 1:34:07 During his remarks before a large gathering of guests that included survivors, first responders and family members of the victims, Trump honored the 184 victims of the attack on the Pentagon, the 2,573 who died in the World Trade Center attack and the 33 passengers who fought against their attackers on United Airlines Flight 93 over Shanksville, Pennsylvania. "Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago: we will never, ever forget," Trump said. The president also took time to honor all those who responded to the attacks in various capacities — both at the time of the attacks and in the years after — as well as those serving overseas today. "For 25 years, our best and bravest have kept America safe, and today, we salute every member of the United States military who served in the war on terror. … We salute our first responders and law enforcement — and we love them — and we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world's No. 1 sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never have a nuclear weapon," Trump said. Hegseth also spoke highly of those who are currently serving and those who have served over the past 25 years. "The top 1% of Americans — those that wear the uniform — still keep the watch, [and] we all sleep in peace because we know they stand ready," he said. The secretary added that, strengthened by faith, the military will continue to defeat the enemies of the U.S. and protect the republic, "just as the heroes and warriors of 9/11 did. Because, in this nation, in God we trust — in this land, in this place, on [9/11] — and still today," he said. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} During his remarks, Caine reflected on being present at the Pentagon the day of the attacks, and on the many selfless acts he observed amid the chaos. "So many of us that day, who were here, saw courageous Americans giving that gift. And to the survivors and the families here today, your presence honors those that we lost … and reminds us of your strength — that we continued forward in this building, in New York, and around the country during one of our darkest chapters," Caine said. "We can't restore what was taken from us that day, but we can make and continue to hold a solemn promise: never to forget," he added. Rice spoke about her time in Washington on 9/11 and the resilience she saw afterward. "It is fitting that here at the Pentagon, we reflect not just on what happened here, but what — in that moment of crisis — people did here. They summoned a will and a spirit: a sense of obligation that our military lives by every day," she said. Prior to the remarks, the names of each of the 184 victims who lost their lives at the Pentagon were read aloud. The ceremony was preceded by an early-morning unfurling of the same American flag that was draped over the building's west wall the day after the 2001 attack. 13:10 Spotlight: Remembering September 11, 2001: 25 Years Later Experience: National 9/11 Pentagon Memorial Video: Pentagon Marks 25th Anniversary of 9/11 Video: Trump, DOW Leaders Host 9/11 Observance Ceremony

title: Hegseth Attends First Space Academy Commission Meeting
text: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth traveled to NASA's headquarters in Washington today where he attended the first meeting of the presidential commission on the U.S. Space Academy. President Donald J. Trump called for the development of a space academy via an Aug. 28 executive order . The order states that the space domain is critical to national security and that the nation must prepare the next generation of space professionals — including those in the military — in order to defend national interests. The commission, which is chaired by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, brings together senior leaders from the War Department, the Office of Management and Budget, and the National Security Council. During his brief remarks at the meeting's outset, Hegseth praised Isaacman and Air Force Secretary Troy Meink — both of whom attended — as well as President Trump for their leadership in getting the counsel assembled and on the path toward developing a space academy. "We are full speed ahead on this partnership on the United States Space Academy and the need for it. The president's been a leader in this domain from the beginning: the Space Force in the first term, [the] Space Academy in the second term," Hegseth said. Trump established the Space Force, which falls under the Department of the Air Force, Dec. 20, 2019, when the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2020 was signed into law. Hegseth went on to say that space is a domain that the U.S. can't just be "good at." "We need to dominate [in space]; and it's not just what we do at the War Department — it's what we do across government, at NASA, in private industry, in collaboration at every echelon," he said. "And so, we see this academy as a key component of ensuring we don't just lead, but we dominate." During his opening statement, Isaacson said that the U.S. is currently in another space race, namely with China and Russia, and that "success and failure comes down to months, not years." "This is why I think President Trump created the Space Force in his first term … and why now he has charged us to create the United States Space Academy: to make sure we have this training ground for the next generation of technicians, engineers, operators, pilots and astronauts to serve the needs of NASA, as well as the Space Force and other government agencies," he said. "Having an academy where we can train the next generation of space professionals — whether it be civilian or military — is just critically important," Meink said during his remarks. "So, we are really looking forward to working with [NASA] to make sure that happens, as well as just the increasing partnership we have [with] NASA across the board. ... I'm really looking forward to [the collaboration]." Per the executive order, the committee has until late December of this year to submit a report to the president proposing key details for the establishment of the academy. title: Department of War Announces Navy's First Advanced Nuclear Microreactor Deployment at Naval Weapons Station Crane, Indiana
text: The Department of War announced the planned installation of the State of Indiana's first advanced nuclear Micro Modular Reactor (MMR) at Naval Weapons Station (NWS) Crane no later than September 2028. This action implements President Donald J. Trump's Executive Orders, Deploying Advanced Nuclear Reactor Technologies for National Security and Reinvigorating the Nuclear Industrial Base, which advances a clear mandate to restore American nuclear leadership globally, remove barriers to innovation, and rebuild the domestic nuclear workforce. The overall project is being executed jointly by the Army's Janus Program, the Office of the Assistant Secretary of the Navy for Energy, Installations and Environment, the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering (OUSW(R&E)), and the State of Indiana. Together, these partners will secure continuous power for one of the Nation's most important defense technology and weapons installations, create highly skilled American jobs, strengthen the American nuclear supply chain, and rebuild the industrial capacity required for national defense. The commercially owned and operated MMR at NWS Crane, one of the United States' premier warfighting innovation and capability development hubs, marks the first step in a larger, unified Department-wide effort to deploy safe and secure nuclear power for national security. The MMR installation will provide reliable, around-the-clock power independent of the commercial electric grid, capable of sustaining critical operations under the most demanding conditions. As the first power-producing reactor installed in Indiana, this project expands the United States' power generation capacity and modernizes the energy infrastructure needed to serve local communities and advance missions critical to national security. The MMR installation is being executed through the Army's Janus Program, in coordination with the Department of the Navy, the Department of War Innovation Unit, and the Office of the Assistant Secretary of War for Critical Technologies (OASW(CT)). This cross-service effort brings together the Army's role as the Department's executive agent for installation nuclear energy, the Navy's operational mission at NWS Crane, DIU's access to commercial innovation, and the Department's critical technology enterprise. "Under President Trump's bold leadership, the Department of War is rapidly fielding next-generation energy solutions for our warfighters," said Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering. "We are unleashing the American nuclear industrial base to ensure our military installations possess the resilient infrastructure required to maintain uninterrupted operations." OASW(CT) is leading the coordination of key stakeholders across the Department to integrate and execute the Crane project under the Janus Program. "At Critical Technologies, we start from a simple first principle: a technology matters only when it reaches the mission," said Mike Dodd, Assistant Secretary of War for Critical Technologies. "Our standard is to field and deploy capability within 24 months or less. President Trump's Executive Order gave the Department a clear mandate to move advanced nuclear power from promise to deployment. We turned that mandate into a focused sprint within our Contested Logistics Critical Technology Area to deliver this capability on time and on target, strengthen the American nuclear industrial base, and secure a decisive advantage for our warfighters." "Janus was designed from the beginning to deliver capability beyond the Army," said the Honorable W. Jordan Gillis, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment. "This partnership demonstrates what is possible when we combine the Army's nuclear expertise and regulatory authorities with the operational installation requirements of our sister Services and the innovation of American industry. Together, we are building a pathway to resilient nuclear power that can strengthen mission assurance across the Joint Force." "Energy security is warfighting capability. Hosting the Navy's first shore-based advanced microreactor at NWS Crane under the Janus Program underscores our commitment to hardening our shore infrastructure against evolving physical, cyber, and grid vulnerabilities," said the Honorable Brendan Rogers, Assistant Secretary of the Navy for Energy, Installations and Environment. "Partnering with the Army and OASW(CT) allows us to move with speed, establish a resilient firm power backbone, and protect the vital research, development, and manufacturing our Fleet depends on every day." This initiative builds on more than a year of close coordination between the Department of War and Indiana state leadership. Senator Jim Banks has been an indispensable partner in advancing the MMR initiative from concept to installation in the Hoosier State. His leadership, together with the direct support of Governor Mike Braun, Senator Todd Young, Representative Erin Houchin, and Representative Mark Messmer, has cleared the path for the Department to move with speed to secure our national defense infrastructure. The Department will continue to work with Federal, state, and local partners throughout the required safety, environmental, regulatory, and installation processes. Nuclear safety, physical security, cybersecurity, and responsible stewardship of taxpayer resources will remain central at every stage. This project marks the first milestone of President Trump's mandate to revitalize the American nuclear industrial base and deploy next-generation energy technologies to secure an enduring advantage for the Joint Force.

title: Rebuilding Defense Industrial Base Requires Skilled Labor
text: To remain competitive, the United States must rebuild its defense industrial base — the private sector companies that provide the military with hardware and munitions — and that means more than just facilities and businesses. That was the message delivered by Michael Cadenazzi, the assistant secretary of war for industrial base policy, during a field hearing before the House Appropriations Committee's defense subcommittee in Santa Clarita, California, Sept. 4. He noted that rebuilding the defense industrial base also means having the right people lining up to do the skilled work at those facilities, such as welding and machining. Machinist Shop Ryan Hughes uses a lathe to machine a submarine part in the Trident Refit Facility Bangor machinist shop at Naval Base Kitsap-Bangor, Wash., April 10, 2026. The War Department recently launched an initiative to encourage young people to choose careers in skilled trades. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.01 MB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 2nd Class Jonathan Estrada-Eguizabal VIRIN: 260410-N-FQ639-1030 "My focus here today is on the skilled tradespeople we need to rebuild and scale the [defense industrial base]: the engineers, the pipe fitters, the welders and those who make the world's finest weapons for our warfighters," Cadenazzi said. Through a variety of initiatives, the War Department has made it a priority to encourage young Americans to choose skilled trades to provide the workforce needed to rebuild America's industrial base. "Decades of government policy and societal pressure have driven millions of talented young Americans toward degrees, which haven't delivered the benefits they were promised, and have left defense manufacturers with few skilled workers waiting in the wings," Cadenazzi said. The secretary said there are some 400,000 unfilled skilled-trade jobs in the defense industrial base today, and that number could grow to 2.5 million over the next decade. Getting Americans into those jobs means convincing young people that skilled-trades work is good work, and meaningful; it is a tall order, he said. "We need to reach Americans in their living rooms and classrooms, break the stigma of blue-collar work and drive a massive influx of passionate, capable people into these programs," Cadenazzi said. The next workforce that will work in the trades and fill skilled labor positions, he said, is in grade school right now. Those young people need to be reached now to pique their interest. "Our approach is that if you don't get kids excited in elementary [and] middle school about the trades, by the time that they graduate high school, they're not actually interested," Cadenazzi said. "[Our] next generation of submarine builders is in middle school today ... so we've got to get them excited in the moment." He noted that one potential hurdle will be parents, who may be reluctant to encourage their children to choose a path other than continuing their education in college, because they may themselves be the first in their families to have attended. "The idea of their kid going to the trades needs to be something they consider," he said. "We need to help the parents understand that this is a great alternative for their children for the future." Vital Trades Aidan Pacheco, a welder at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Maine, performs a vital weld on a steel trailer, July 7, 2026. The War Department wants more young people to choose careers in the skilled trades. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.04 MB ) Credit: Neil Boorjian, Navy VIRIN: 260707-N-FQ573-1023 Earlier this summer, the War Department launched the Build Freedom Initiative, which promotes and funds blue-collar careers. Through the initiative, coupled with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's arsenal of freedom effort, the department aims to strengthen the nation by encouraging more Americans to choose the skilled-trade workforce. For the War Department, that means rebuilding the defense industrial base, including training more young Americans to build and repair ships, aircraft and munitions. "Build Freedom will act as a national hiring, training and awareness campaign to drive America's resurgence in defense manufacturing," Cadenazzi told lawmakers. "Build Freedom aligns more than 70 industrial-based analysis and sustainment, or IBAS, workforce projects under one campaign, ensuring that federally funded workforce opportunities reach the Americans they were designed to serve." The Build Freedom Initiative was initially launched in three states — Texas, Michigan and Pennsylvania — and DOW plans to expand the program nationwide. "This national awareness will drive individuals to our new buildfreedom.us website, a one-stop shop where their interests can be converted into scholarships, training, credentials and job opportunities," Cadenazzi said. "Our goal with Build Freedom is to send a clear, compelling message to the American public: there are hundreds of thousands of good-paying, [artificial intelligence-proof] jobs available today in the [defense industrial base] and in other skilled trades." 2:27:09 Story: Build Freedom Initiative Launches With Big Contract to Skilled Trades Champion Spotlight: Acquisition Transformation Experience: Delivering Peace Through Strength Spotlight: DOW Innovates

title: Army Garrison Prepares for Milestone 9/11 Commemoration
text: A quarter of a century after the tragic events of Sept. 11, 2001, U.S. Army Garrison Italy soldiers, military police and firefighters will gather alongside local Italian officials in Padua, Italy, for a solemn 25th anniversary commemoration at the Memory and Light memorial. World Trade Center Beam A steel beam from the World Trade Center wreckage is displayed as part of the Memory and Light memorial during a 9/11 remembrance ceremony in Padua, Italy, Sept. 11, 2025. U.S. service members gathered alongside Italian partners to commemorate the 24th anniversary of the attack. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 266.24 KB ) Credit: Army Sgt. Salvador Castro VIRIN: 250911-A-JH229-1904 "Returning to [Padua] for this milestone 25th anniversary observance will allow us to pay tribute to the lives lost and honor the enduring strength of our alliance," said Army Col. Vaughn D. Strong Jr., U.S. Army Garrison Italy commander. "Our soldiers and firemen look forward to standing together with our Italian partners to ensure the legacy of that day is never forgotten." Designed by Daniel Libeskind, the world renowned architect behind the ground zero master plan in New York City, the memorial features a 55-foot glass structure shaped like an open book, its "pages" pointing directly toward New York and the Statue of Liberty. Enclosed within the glass is a 19-foot twisted steel beam recovered from the wreckage of the World Trade Center, one of Europe's most poignant physical ties to the site. For leaders, the anniversary underscores the shared values that bind American and Italian first responders. "Having this piece of ground zero right here in Veneto, just down the road from where we serve at Caserma Ederle and Del Din, is profoundly meaningful," said Luca Giaretta, deputy fire chief for USAG Italy fire and emergency services. "It serves as a physical touchstone connecting our local Italian community with our American military colleagues, reminding us why our daily partnership and joint readiness matter so much." 9/11 Ceremony U.S. service members and Italian partners attend a 9/11 remembrance ceremony in Padua, Italy, Sept. 11, 2025. Strong Jr., left, U.S. Army Garrison Italy commander, and Army Command Sgt. Maj. Ricardo Moreno, right, the garrison's senior enlisted advisor, alongside Italian officials render a salute during a 9/11 remembrance ceremony in Padua, Italy, Sept. 11, 2025. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 389.12 KB ) Credit: Army Sgt. Salvador Castro VIRIN: 250911-A-JH229-6602 Harold R. Persons, fire chief for USAG Italy fire and emergency services, emphasized the depth of that connection. "We are deeply appreciative of [the local fire department] for their continuous efforts to memorialize and show their respect for not only the 343 firefighters, but all 412 emergency workers and the 2,753 civilians who lost their lives in the horrific attack at the World Trade Center," he said. "Sharing in this annual remembrance ceremony with our fellow firefighters, police and other emergency responders at the memorial site in [Padua] honors the sacrifice of those who gave their lives attempting to save others." As the decades pass, ceremonies at the memorial take on new significance for younger generations of military members and firefighters who were not yet born in 2001. Army Lt. Col. Jonathan Kuhn, provost marshal and director of garrison emergency services, highlighted how the milestone bridges the past and future for today's service members. Memory and Light The Memory and Light memorial stands behind U.S., Italian and European Union flags during a 9/11 commemoration in Padua, Italy, Sept. 11, 2025. The site, anchored by a steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center, serves as one of Europe's most powerful tributes to the victims of 9/11 and the enduring U.S.-Italy partnership. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.88 MB ) Credit: Anna Ciccotti, Army VIRIN: 250911-A-NR142-9981 "Marking 25 years at the 9/11 monument reminds today's military police, soldiers and first responders that our mission is rooted in sacrifice, vigilance and service to something larger than ourselves," he said. "For those serving now, it is both a tribute to those who answered the call after 9/11 and a renewed commitment to protecting our communities with professionalism, discipline and readiness." Kuhn added that standing side by side with Italian partners sends a clear message to the local community. "I hope they see a shared commitment to remembrance, resilience and service," he said. "American and Italian crews standing side by side at the monument sends a simple message: tragedy can cross borders, but so can solidarity, partnership and the duty to stand together in its aftermath." Ultimately, the commemoration ensures that the standard set on 9/11 endures. As Kuhn noted, "Ceremonies like this help make sure 9/11 is not just something younger firefighters read about but something they feel connected to as part of their professional identity. They reinforce that duty, sacrifice and service to others are not abstract ideals; they are the standard we inherit and the one we are responsible for carrying forward." title: Joint Interagency Task Force 401 Publishes Counter-UAS Reference Guide
text: Joint Interagency Task Force 401 recently published its 2026 Counter-Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Quick Reference Guide , establishing a shared baseline of technical and tactical knowledge across the joint force and interagency partners. Aerial Target A soldier assigned to the 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry Regiment, 1st Cavalry Division, uses cord to attach a polyvinyl chloride pipe and a balloon to a drone, creating a simulated aerial target for a counter-small unmanned aircraft system during a training exercise at Fort Hood, Texas, July 15, 2026. Joint Interagency Task Force 401 recently published the 2026 Counter-Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Quick Reference Guide to help planners and tactical operators understand their equipment's full capabilities. It translates high-level strategic doctrine into concrete, repeatable tactics, techniques and procedures, enabling synchronized defenses against a rapidly evolving threat. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 2.48 MB ) Credit: Army Staff Sgt. Zelika Stewart VIRIN: 260717-A-ZS678-1003 "The proliferation of unmanned aircraft systems is creating new challenges at home and abroad," said Army Brig. Gen. Matthew Ross, task force director. "There is no silver bullet or single solution to address this challenge. This [quick reference guide] is a practical tool to help leaders and operators understand the [counter-UAS] landscape, apply lessons learned and rapidly put effective solutions into the hands of warfighters and other security personnel." The task force developed the guide to help planners and tactical operators understand their equipment's full capabilities. It translates high-level strategic doctrine into concrete, repeatable tactics, techniques and procedures, enabling synchronized defenses against a rapidly evolving threat. "A [quick reference guide] like this benefits everyone," said Air Force Col. Jonathan M. Beha, the data, analysis, requirements and training division chief for JIATF 401. "Operators have a concise guide to reference and build their tactics, policymakers new to the [counter-UAS] mission have a starting place for learning, and the broader community is able to seek out more information." The document includes a lessons learned section that shares real-world tactical outcomes. This direct feedback loop between frontline operators and developers ensures defensive strategies and training evolve as quickly as the threat, preventing repeated tactical mistakes and improving operational security. With low-cost commercial drones in Ukraine and the Middle East fundamentally changing the battlefield, combatant commands worldwide face a variety of aerial threats that now include both state and nonstate actors. To defend against these threats, the guide provides a common technical baseline for sensors, command and control, and intercepting drones in groups 1-3 in deployed and homeland settings. By establishing clear, repeatable tactics, it establishes common operational language, allowing military and interagency teams to coordinate quickly and effectively. Formatted as a tactical pocket guide, the quick reference guide ensures that defensive strategies, capabilities and training methods can adapt as rapidly as emerging drone technologies. title: Cadets Explore Potential Army Careers During Branch Week
text: Representatives from 16 Army branches provided members of the U.S. Military Academy's Corps of Cadets a glimpse into what they may encounter after graduation and commissioning during Branch Week, Aug. 24-28 at West Point, New York. Branch Week A cadet looks through the scope of a weapon while at an Army branch static display during Branch Week at West Point, N.Y., Aug. 24-28, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 245.76 KB ) Credit: Eric Bartelt, United States Military Academy at West Point VIRIN: 260826-O-ZV784-1433 The annual knowledge-gathering event allows cadet candidates from the U.S. Military Academy Preparatory School and the West Point community to enjoy static displays and informational booths presented by each branch representing functions across the Army. The five-day event culminated with a Capability Exercise, bringing those capabilities to life as soldiers and cadets demonstrated Army power and lethality before spectators. Upper-class cadets took a deeper look at their top two branch choices through engagement sessions with officers and noncommissioned officers, helping them make more informed decisions about their future Army careers. Among the officers who came to West Point for Branch Week was Army Capt. Wilson Catoe, a 2022 USMA graduate and former Army West Point football player. Catoe works for the U.S. Army Infantry School and the Office of the Chief of the Infantry as an Infantry branch proponent officer. "Ultimately, I am the decision maker as to which cadets, either USMA or ROTC, and [Officer Candidate School] will branch in the Infantry, and who does not," said Catoe, who formerly served as a platoon leader and executive officer assigned to the 1st Battalion, 67th Armor Regiment, 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team, at Fort Bliss, Texas. In speaking with cadets about the Infantry Branch, Catoe emphasized its central role in the Army, describing it as "the heart and soul of the Army" and "the main effort of the Army force." "If you want an opportunity to challenge yourself physically and mentally in any demand of any environment, then the Infantry is for you," Catoe said. "The opportunity to lead America's sons and daughters against any adversary, it paints a picture of the high standards that the Infantry holds." Catoe said being in the Infantry was a chance to see himself grow exponentially. "It's a humbling opportunity to come back to West Point and see people share the same experience you did, and leading them into such a highly demanding branch," Catoe said. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} To have a positive influence on a cadet's career choice, Catoe describes it as "the responsibility of a lifetime" with the goal of welcoming new blood into the branch. As a cadet, Catoe had a tunnel-vision focus on what USMA expected, going to class and making sure his grades were up to par to stay on the football team. However, Branch Week offered an experience to meet with U.S. Army Forces Command units and understand all the opportunities afforded to them throughout the Army. "When everybody comes out and hears the pitches of each branch, cadets are able to grow and understand," Catoe said. "Those who serve in the branch share their experiences, so the cadets can understand what they're getting into in the Army." Another officer who helped cadets find perspective on their future branches was Army 1st Lt. Sam Hanson, assigned to the Field Artillery Proponent Office stationed at Fort Sill, Oklahoma, where they handle accessions for cadets from across the country. The most important thing Hanson wanted to convey to cadets was that every branch, not specifically Field Artillery, is "important to the fight that we're trying to win." He talked about three unique jobs offered in Field Artillery where "each of those jobs requires a completely different skill set. "Hanson said most cadets wanted to hear what a typical day is like for a Field Artillery lieutenant and how the branch will change over time. "In the next five years, we expect to field two new weapon systems that are going to completely change the way we fight the close fight," Hanson said. "They're really interested in that transition and being a part of that monumental change." The Wake Forest University ROTC graduate talked about recruiting talent to their unique branch, but first and foremost said the Army is a people's business. "This is what you are going to do for however long you're in the military, and so it's really important that you identify with the people you're talking to," Hanson said. "I always tell cadets, pick what feels right to you." Branch Week Chemical Corps Branch representatives dressed in protective gear discuss the Army's chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear defense with a U.S. Military Academy cadet during Branch Week at West Point, N.Y., Aug. 24-28, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 286.72 KB ) Credit: Kyle Osterhoudt, United States Military Academy at West Point VIRIN: 260825-O-CL008-3916 Class of 2027 Cadet Samuel Eppler believes Branch Week is a remarkable experience for all cadets. "I remember coming in plebe year after finishing Beast, and thinking the Army was the whole branch and there was just an infantry," Eppler said. "Coming here and seeing all the different branches, it gave me a unique perspective of how interwoven all the branches in the Army are, and how they rely on each other for supply or whether it be combat arms or maneuver elements." "It really opened my eyes to all the possibilities that the Army offers," he added. "Then, in the future, the possible career paths I can choose." The American Politics major from Ionia, Michigan, is hoping to branch into Aviation and potentially fly the UH-60 Black Hawk. As part of Branch Week, senior class cadets participated in engagement sessions with their top two branch choices. Eppler attended sessions for Aviation and Explosive Ordnance Disposal. His interest in EOD grew after spending part of the summer at Cadet Troop Leader Training with an EOD unit at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. "EOD has really technical skills that you learn through that branch," Eppler said. "I thought it was extraordinary." Regardless of which path he ultimately chooses, the best piece of advice he received from Army officers that stuck with him was "there are no bad branches in the Army." "With anything you do, it's always about service to your country," Eppler said. "So, there's always a fulfillment that you can get within each branch." Branch Week allows cadets to see how each branch achieves the Army's mission. Eppler said the experience of seeing each branch and some of the Army's equipment was "amazing." "This experience not only shows where the Army is at now, but talking with different officers and enlisted people, you can see the future direction of the Army with the technology that we're producing for combat with lessons learned in Ukraine and other areas around the globe," he said. For Eppler, bringing the branches together at West Point allows cadets to learn about parts of the Army they may not experience during summer training. "It's perfect how West Point does it and puts [branches] all together," he said. "You walk down the strip and talk to different people from different branches, and it's very educational for each cadet. During summer training, you don't get the hands-on with some of these different branches, but for this environment to provide you with a lot more insight into the daily job and the mission set of each branch — it's incredible." title: Guard Program Links Global Partnership to DOW Priorities
text: Senior leaders and security cooperation personnel from across the War Department gathered for the 2026 National Guard Bureau State Partnership Program conference in Atlanta, Aug. 13. The goal of the annual conference was to align activities and engagements with National Defense Strategy Lines of Effort, administration arms transfer reform objectives and rigorous data-driven evaluation to prove return on investment for the American taxpayer. Combat Readiness Indiana National Guard soldiers assigned to the 1st Battalion, 151st Infantry Regiment, and Slovak Armed Forces soldiers conduct an assault on an objective during a combat readiness exercise near Butlerville, Ind., July 26, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.91 MB ) Credit: Army Staff Sgt. DeWayne Johnson VIRIN: 260726-Z-DT466-4123 In addition to DOW, the event included speakers from the Defense Security Cooperation Agency, Defense Security Cooperation University and the National Guard Bureau's International Affairs Directorate, including the assessment, monitoring and evaluation, foreign disclosure and integration teams. Throughout the event, speakers tied ongoing SPP achievements to the four NDS LOEs: defend the Homeland; deter China in the Pacific region through strength, not confrontation; increase burden-sharing with U.S. allies and partners; and supercharge the U.S. defense industrial base. Keynote speaker Christopher Mamaux, deputy assistant secretary of war for security cooperation, highlighted the program's critical role in operationalizing national security objectives. "As we look to the future, we must transition our partnerships from a default of security dependence to operational independence," Mamaux said. "We want to focus our energy on developing model allies, partners who are willing to spend on their own defense and contribute meaningfully to regional security." Mamaux emphasized the asymmetric advantage built over decades of state-level engagement. "With 117 partner nations, we have built a network of trust over decades that our strategic competitors cannot hope to replicate," he said. David Ferrari, the Defense Security Cooperation Agency advisor to the director, focused on the intersection of the SPP and the defense industrial ecosystem under Executive Order 14383, the America First Arms Transfer Strategy. Ferrari characterized guard personnel in the field as an "early-warning system" for foreign military sales requirements. "This is exactly where the SPP's persistent engagement is a strategic enabler, as you are in these countries year after year and can help partners identify what they need before they submit a request," he said, noting that this operational alignment creates a reinforcing cycle between procurement and capability development. "As we improve FMS processes to help partners buy more U.S. equipment, we are directly scaling the arena for SPP activities," Ferrari said. He concluded with a direct call to action for guard leaders to leverage partner investment to strengthen mutual readiness. Partnership Program Air Force Senior Master Sgt. Steven Dauck, a flight chief assigned to Hawaii Air National Guard's 154th Explosive Ordnance Disposal Flight, shows an OG-9 recoilless training weapon to Indonesian Air Force personnel at Andersen Air Force Base, Guam, July 22, 2026. Hawaii National Guard service members routinely train with their Indonesian Air Force counterparts through the State Partnership Program, which aims to enhance disaster response, aviation, medical readiness, cybersecurity and professional development between the partner nations. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.82 MB ) Credit: Air Force Senior Airman Roann Gatdula VIRIN: 260722-Z-KH177-1003 "As you conduct your persistent engagements this year, look at your partners through the lens of [the America First Arms Transfer Strategy]," he said. "Help us identify where partner capital can invest in mutual capacity, and help us transition them to modern, standard U.S. systems. We cannot reindustrialize the arsenal of freedom without the guard leading the way on the ground." Regarding workforce development, Sonya Finley, the dean of workforce education and development at the Defense Security Cooperation University, outlined key milestones in the professionalization of security cooperation. Under DSCU, the SPP has been officially designated as a distinct functional area within the War Department's Security Cooperation Workforce Certification 2.0 Program — a major step toward codifying and standardizing global partnership management across the joint force. Conference sessions also underscored the importance of maintaining high-quality data processes. Recent policy guidance has institutionalized assessment, monitoring and evaluation as a mandatory mechanism to measure performance, demonstrate accountability and justify resourcing for SPP activities. Mamaux reinforced that strategic alignment applies directly to resource stewardship. "We must prove that our resources are aligned with the NDS lines of effort and provide a very clear return on our investment," he said. "Every dollar you spend across the program must be logical, transparent and benefit the American people." Partners in the Skies Air Force Staff Sgt. Jack Heintz, a crew chief assigned to the New York Air National Guard's 106th Maintenance Squadron, describes the capabilities of an HC-130J Combat King II aircraft to Swedish Air Force Cpl. Wincent Enhörning, a helicopter mechanic assigned to Malmen Air Base in Linköping, Sweden, Aug. 20, 2026. New York National Guard members are in Sweden for events surrounding the Swedish Air Force's centennial jubilee and engagements through the National Guard State Partnership Program. In one instance, military planners maximized space on existing training transport to deliver equipment to Albania, achieving a critical delivery while eliminating commercial transportation costs. title: Army Lasers Blast Drones, Proving Directed-Energy Weapons Are Future
text: Protecting the Homeland Joint Task Force Southern Border personnel use the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser system to engage and defeat three hostile unmanned aerial systems along the U.S. southern border, Aug. 25, 2026. Approximately 8,000 service members are currently deployed as part of the task force to protect U.S. territorial integrity by boosting awareness, accelerating response and supporting federal law enforcement partners. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 389.12 KB ) Credit: Army Sgt. Daniel Huerta VIRIN: 260826-D-D0945-3729 Earlier this week, service members assigned to Joint Task Force Southern Border used the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser system to stop three hostile, unmanned aircraft systems deemed a threat. They were believed to be linked to drug cartels. "The successful defeat of these adversarial drones is a direct testament to the readiness, vigilance and technological edge of the [joint task force]," said Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, Joint Task Force Southern Border commander. "By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance." The operation marks the first use of the laser system to defeat cartel-linked drones along the southern border. Using directed-energy weapons, such as this, is part of the future of warfare, a War Department official said. "The future of warfare obviously is going to include mass attritable drones," the official added. The department will procure hundreds of thousands of drones as soon as next year, as well as counter-UAS technology, including directed-energy systems. "The department is proliferating directed-energy technology to protect the homeland and the southern border," the official said. "And [U.S. Northern Command and Joint Task Force Southern Border are] deploying these capabilities to take out any ... cartel drones that are doing incursions at the border." Directed-energy weapons, such as lasers, can be used to take out both drones and incoming cruise missiles, at a much lower cost than using more expensive kinetic weapons like missiles. Developing scaled directed energy weapons systems, such as what was used at the border, is one of the department's six critical technology areas. The other areas include: applied artificial intelligence, biomanufacturing, contested logistics technologies, quantum and battlefield information dominance, and scaled hypersonics. "[Directed-energy systems are] low cost per shot, with deep magazines and they can come out against drone swarms," the official said. "That's something that's different than a traditional kinetic system. It's good for the cost-exchange ratio because ... it's better than us firing a $2 million missile at [an inexpensive] drone." The use of directed-energy weapons on drones is also in line with the department's counter-drone effort, the official noted. By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance." Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, Joint Task Force Southern Border commander In June, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth visited White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico, where he observed a variety of directed-energy systems in operation, including the first milestone test of the Golden Dome for America. "Cutting-edge directed energy was harnessed, and the Dynamic Defense Autonomous Defeat system flawlessly and autonomously cued, targeted and eliminated a multitude of incoming threats," the secretary said. "This test was executed on schedule and dynamically defeated every threat. I watched our elite warfighters integrate with next-generation technology to stop incoming drones and cruise missiles dead in their tracks." In July, the War Department awarded two agreements under the Joint Laser Weapon System program to advance the next-generation cruise missile and unmanned aerial system defense architecture. The agreements have an initial award value of $86 million and a total program ceiling of $847 million. The Joint Laser Weapon System program is meant to transition directed-energy capabilities from demonstration prototypes into field-ready, production-oriented platforms. "We must actively defend the homeland against emerging threats," said Emil Michael, undersecretary of war for research and engineering and chief technology officer for the War Department. "We are partnering with industry to rapidly deliver deep magazine directed energy capabilities to the joint force that can be seamlessly deployed across multiple domains." title: Sky Soldiers Train for Modern Conflict in Europe's Premier Crucible Event
text: More than 2,300 paratroopers assigned to the 173rd Airborne Brigade, along with more than 2,100 allied and partner forces from 10 nations are participating in Exercise Saber Junction 26 at the Joint Multinational Readiness Center in Hohenfels, Germany. Saber Junction A soldier assigned to Joint Multinational Readiness Center's Cherokee Company, 1st Battalion, 4th Infantry Regiment, pulls security during Exercise Saber Junction 26 at the Joint Multinational Readiness Center's Hohenfels Training Area in Germany, Aug. 26, 2026. Exercise Saber Junction 26 tests the brigade's ability to rapidly deploy, conduct joint forcible entry, execute offensive and defensive operations, and regenerate combat power in a contested environment. The exercise incorporates lessons learned from ongoing conflicts, including electronic warfare, unmanned aerial systems, dispersed maneuver and contested communications. Southern European Task Force, Africa serves as the division-level higher command for the rotation, integrating U.S. and allied formations, issuing division orders, maintaining the common operating picture, and rehearsing mission command essential for operations across Europe and Africa. "Saber Junction is where our soldiers and our allies prove they are ready for the demands of modern war," said Army Maj. Gen. Matthew W. Brown, Southern European Task Force, Africa commander.
