title: Review Panel Continues Its Mission as Pentagon Marks Fifth Anniversary of Abbey Gate Bombing
text: Senior Advisor to the Secretary of War Sean Parnell revealed in a social media post today that an ongoing War Department investigation into the circumstances surrounding the 2021 terrorist airport bombing in Kabul, Afghanistan, has uncovered classified documents that had not been previously located. Airport Security Army paratroopers assigned to the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 82nd Airborne Division, conduct security as they facilitate the evacuation of U.S. citizens, special immigrant visa applicants and other at-risk Afghans out of Afghanistan as quickly and safely as possible at Hamid Karzai International Airport in Kabul, Aug. 25, 2021. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 4.7 MB ) Credit: Army Master Sgt. Alexander Burnett VIRIN: 210825-A-UV471-113A Parnell gave the update on the fifth anniversary of the suicide bombing attack at then-Hamid Karzai International Airport's Abbey Gate, which killed 13 U.S. service members and approximately 170 Afghan civilians. "Recently, my team recovered highly relevant classified documents — material that should have been disclosed — stashed and hidden away in safes where they would not be found," Parnell said, adding that, once the documents were discovered and examined by a special review panel, "it became clear why someone tried to hide them." An update from Sean Parnell, Chairman of the Afghanistan Withdrawal Special Review Panel, on the Fifth Anniversary of the Abbey Gate bombing pic.twitter.com/5pkbmuuyX0 — Sean Parnell (@SeanParnellASW) August 26, 2026 Parnell went on to say that he didn't want to disclose the contents of the classified documents prematurely. "I'm not going to give you a convenient version of the truth, nor will I give you a rushed one. Here is my commitment: We are following the evidence to wherever it leads and to whoever it touches. We're not accepting incomplete or comfortable answers," he said. One year ago, on the fourth anniversary of the attack and while surrounded by Gold Star family members of the victims in the Oval Office, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced that Parnell — himself a veteran of the war in Afghanistan — had been selected to lead the special review panel looking into the attack and that the ongoing review was taking place on behalf of the American people and on behalf of the Gold Star families. Thirteen Roses Thirteen roses, two pink and eleven white, rest on the pedestal of the United States Marine Corps War Memorial in Arlington, Va., Aug. 28, 2021, representing the thirteen U.S. service members who lost their lives while assisting non-combatant evacuation screening at Abbey Gate of Hamid Karzai International Airport in Kabul, Afghanistan. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.68 MB ) Credit: Marine Corps Staff Sgt. Kelly L. Timney VIRIN: 210828-M-OU200-1052 "America deserves answers as far as what happened in Afghanistan," Hegseth said. "The military needs to answer for what happened." During his address on social media, Parnell spoke highly of the panel members, noting that they have extensive military service in Afghanistan. "These patriots commanded troops; they took fire; they carried the wounded, and they buried their friends," he said. "They knew how decisions in Afghanistan became consequences because they are the ones who lived with them." Airport Security An Afghan man hands his child to a British paratrooper assigned to the 2nd Battalion, Parachute Regiment, while a U.S. service member assigned to the Army's 1st Brigade Combat Team, 82nd Airborne Division, conducts security at Hamid Karzai International Airport in Kabul, Afghanistan, Aug. 26, 2021. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 3.97 MB ) Credit: Army Master Sgt. Alexander Burnett VIRIN: 210826-A-UV471-211 The establishment of the special review panel followed U.S. Central Command's supplemental review in April 2024, which revisited the military's original investigation into the attack. That review, which identified the lone suicide attacker as a member of ISIS-Khorasan, determined the initial investigation's findings were accurate: that the attack could not have been prevented at the tactical level. Though Parnell did not give a specific timeframe as to when he anticipates the special review panel's work being completed, he did ensure the thoroughness and integrity of its investigation. "The American people and the families who sacrificed everything are owed the full picture of how and why those decisions were made, and we're going to give it to them," he said. "That's a promise — not just for today, not just for an anniversary — but until it's done."

title: Army Armaments Center Unveils New Ammo Packaging System
text: Blending lightweight polymers with a rugged steel shell, the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Armaments Center's new SixPAC system marks a groundbreaking leap in small-caliber ammunition packaging, one intended to reshape how soldiers use munitions. The SixPAC, named for its capacity to hold 6.8 mm cartridges, consists of two lightweight polymer ammunition containers in a steel outer pack. After successful implementation with the cartridges, the system is planned for adaptation across multiple legacy small-caliber ammunition production lines. New SixPAC The U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Armaments Center's next-generation lightweight packaging system, the SixPAC, is built to modernize small-caliber ammunition logistics and reduce weight, costs and supply chain vulnerabilities. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 102.4 KB ) Credit: Eric Kowal, Army VIRIN: 260825-A-GY890-1001 This initiative serves as the first major overhaul of small-caliber ammunition packaging since World War II. Supply chain vulnerabilities, rising costs and a need to prepare for tomorrow's military operations in varied climates necessitated a reevaluation of current munitions packaging. The system is designed with a lighter tactical inner pack, which will broaden its manufacturing base and increase efficiency. The system is defined by the absence of a traditional outer wood box, which often required remediation, had to be assembled manually and was susceptible to mold. It also reduces reliance on chemical wood preservative treatments, lowering environmental impacts and the risk of supply chain disruption. The polymer inner pack reduces weight, enables easier transport and is more efficient to manufacture. The steel outer pack reduces the logistical footprint by allowing more containers and ammunition per pallet and has a notably larger supply base than its legacy wood counterpart. Crucible Training Kyesha T. Siggers, a Marine Corps recruit assigned to Bravo Company, 1st Recruit Training Battalion, passes an ammo can over an obstacle during the crucible training event at Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island, S.C., July 30, 2026. The crucible is the final culminating event recruits must complete before earning the title of Marine. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.37 MB ) Credit: Marine Corps Lance Cpl. Katrina Wallace VIRIN: 260730-M-UA605-1239 Teamwork Makes the Dream Work Marine Corps recruit Kyesha T. Siggers passes an ammo can through an obstacle during the Crucible at Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island, S.C., July 30, 2026. The Crucible is the final culminating event recruits must complete before earning the title of Marine. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 6 MB ) Credit: Marine Corps Lance Cpl. Katrina Wallace VIRIN: 260730-M-UA605-9612 According to the project's technical lead, Jason Runell, the SixPAC was partly driven by a desire to do away with the wooden box and largely pursued to modernize for present-day logistics, portability and supply chain challenges. His team tested several materials and received feedback from various user communities before landing on a polymer inner pack and a steel outer pack. This decision, he added, comes out of necessity — polymers aren't yet as proven in the U.S. as they are in other countries. However, the U.S. must be ready to engage at any time and fight in various climates, all with their own difficulties and needs. To meet military standards, polymers must hold up no matter the locale, even after years of storage. "It's a developing field, and polymers are unique — you can modify them, include additives that improve impact performance, stiffness or dimensional stability," said Edward Lucas, a mechanical engineer and polymer designer at the center. "You can add more ingredients to the cauldron and your potion will come out different, trading some characteristics for others." Several designs are in development, with inner tactical polymer containers expected to weigh about half as much as legacy steel containers. This weight savings will reduce the load on soldiers. The decrease will also be advantageous, particularly on weight-sensitive platforms such as light watercraft and aircraft. Weight affects whether these platforms can launch and plays a part in their agility. Beyond that, injection molding for these inner packs will offer supply chain advantages. More than 800 injection molders in the U.S. can likely produce these packs, creating competition, slashing costs and lowering barriers to entry for new suppliers. Additionally, polymer inner packs can be produced largely through injection molding, where most components are formed in a single custom mold and do not require large dedicated fabrication lines. Because the same press can be used for other products by swapping molds, polymer production requires a much smaller footprint and fewer dedicated tools. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} Soldiers tested the SixPAC throughout 2024-2025 and gave valuable feedback, much of it positive. Several service members pointed out that when aboard watercraft or aircraft, "every ounce counts" and that the new system will allow them to carry more ammunition. The polymer inner pack design is currently undergoing refinement, with an ongoing evaluation of options. The armaments center plans to continue investing in multiple container designs and will share pertinent information, such as performance requirements, dimensional constraints and lessons learned with industry partners. The new SixPAC system represents a critical step toward modernizing ammunition logistics and will allow the War Department to meet future challenges and demands more easily, Runell said. title: EOD Airmen Train on Full Spectrum of Explosive Threats
text: The call comes in from headquarters. "[Explosive ordnance disposal], this is Godfather. Be advised hostiles approaching your location. How copy?" Exercise Big Trouble Air Force Airman 1st Class Levi Womack, an explosive ordnance disposal technician assigned to the 341st Civil Engineer Squadron, reviews recently acquired information about a simulated chemical explosive device during Exercise Big Trouble at Limestone Hills Training Area, Mont., Aug. 18, 2026. Manipulating a device in full protective posture tests a technician's dexterity and composure. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 378.88 KB ) Credit: Air Force Tech. Sgt. Aaron Thomasson VIRIN: 260818-F-NC256-9202 Exercise Big Trouble Air Force Senior Airman Mitchell Massa, front, an explosive ordnance disposal technician assigned to the 366th Civil Engineer Squadron, and Air Force Airman 1st Class Levi Womack, an explosive ordnance disposal technician assigned to the 341st Civil Engineer Squadron, approach a simulated chemical explosive device during Exercise Big Trouble at Limestone Hills Training Area, Mont., Aug. 18, 2026. Working in chemical protective gear adds heat, restricted mobility and limited visibility, conditions technicians must train in to stay effective against contaminated threats. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 512 KB ) Credit: Air Force Tech. Sgt. Aaron Thomasson VIRIN: 260818-F-NC256-9194 Inside the gas mask, every breath feels like drinking air through a straw. Air Force Airman 1st Class Levi Womack keys the radio and responds. "Godfather, this is EOD. Good copy." Further up the ridgeline, Air Force Senior Airman Mitchell Massa hears the radio chatter and knows time is running out. He is working against the clock to disarm and decontaminate a chemical explosive device found in the woods near a forward operating base. With the seconds slipping by, his entire world narrows down to the problem in front of him, visible only through the fogged lenses of his gas mask. Then the call comes in from headquarters to leave the area. Massa works his way down the ridge, moving slowly in his chemical protective gear and drops the device in a decontamination tub. "End of scenario," yells the instructor during Exercise Big Trouble, a weeklong field training exercise at Limestone Hills Training Area near Townsend, Montana. It's only the morning of the first day and Massa and Womack are already drenched in sweat as they peel off their protective gear, hot and thirsty under the August sun. Massa, assigned to the 366th Civil Engineer Squadron at Mountain Home Air Force Base, Idaho, and Womack, assigned to the 341st Civil Engineer Squadron at Malmstrom Air Force Base, Montana, are there to hone their craft on simulated chemicals and explosive devices. They gather around the instructor for a debrief after finishing their second problem of the day. He tells them this scenario is meant to teach junior explosive ordnance disposal technicians what to do when external constraints make it too dangerous to continue disposal operations. Knowing when to break off a mission rather than push past the point of safety was exactly the lesson Air Force Staff Sgt. Lucky Widjaja, the exercise's main organizer and a 341st Civil Engineer Squadron EOD technician, wanted every technician to carry off the range. "The end goal is for them to realize their limitations and capabilities — the miles they're able to travel and how they function under less-than-ideal conditions," Widjaja said. "So that if that were to ever happen in a deployed environment, they have that experience to fall back on." Exercise Big Trouble Air Force Senior Airman Mitchell Massa, an explosive ordnance disposal technician assigned to the 366th Civil Engineer Squadron, operates the controls for a transportable robotic system during Exercise Big Trouble at Limestone Hills Training Area, Mont., Aug. 18, 2026. The system allows EOD teams to investigate and handle suspected devices remotely, keeping technicians outside the blast radius. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 348.16 KB ) Credit: Air Force Tech. Sgt. Aaron Thomasson VIRIN: 260818-F-NC256-9074 Exercise Big Trouble Air Force Airman 1st Class Levi Womack, right, an explosive ordnance disposal technician assigned to the 341st Civil Engineer Squadron, inspects the gas mask of Air Force Senior Airman Mitchell Massa, an explosive ordnance disposal technician assigned to the 366th Civil Engineer Squadron, during Exercise Big Trouble at Limestone Hills Training Area, Mont., Aug. 18, 2026. Confirming a proper mask seal is critical before entering a contaminated environment, where a compromised seal could expose a technician to chemical hazards. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 337.92 KB ) Credit: Air Force Tech. Sgt. Aaron Thomasson VIRIN: 260818-F-NC256-9189 Now in its fourth iteration and second year bringing in EOD airmen from around the country, this year's exercise featured six Air Force EOD teams training in a simulated deployed environment. Over the week, technicians worked though scenarios that spanned a range of threats they could see downrange, such as improvised explosive devices, unexploded ordnance, weapons caches, route denial and chemical agents, like what Massa and Womack confronted that first morning. The training plan was built for airmen early in their careers, many of them working through these high-pressure, decision-making processes for the first time. The aim was to develop technicians who understood what team leadership demanded and could transfer their skills to real-world deployed environments. If judgment, leadership and technical skill were the lessons, communication between EOD shops was the method. Planners paired technicians with counterparts from other shops to trade tactics, techniques and procedures, allowing airmen to sharpen not just their own units but the shops they trained alongside. "My favorite part is getting EOD members from different shops out here to train," Widjaja said. "It allows us to communicate and exchange learning points so that we are, as a whole EOD enterprise, more ready and capable to face our next emerging threat." Throughout the week, teams gained experience with the career field's full toolkit. Massa traded his chemical protective gear for the controls of an unmanned ground vehicle, sending the robot to examine a suspected device while the operator stayed outside the blast radius. In another case, careful planning made success possible. Air Force Staff Sgt. Hartvig Homberg, a 341st Civil Engineer Squadron EOD technician, and Air Force Airman 1st Class Jacob Miller-Lujan, a 28th Civil Engineer Squadron EOD technician from Ellsworth Air Force Base, South Dakota, mapped out a plan before tackling a problem with multiple devices, deciding who did what and in what order. After each scenario, teams gathered to debrief, learning new lessons before moving to the next problem. The training tempo left technicians with limited recovery time. Teams woke up early to prep their gear and were on the range by 8 a.m. Once there, they rotated through problems, trading team leader and team member roles and switching between mounted and dismounted work. After a short rest at the end of the afternoon, they started a night mission brief around 9 p.m. and conducted training while using night-vision devices until at least midnight. For the airmen learning during Big Trouble, the purposeful grind of the exercise teaches not just explosives, but teamwork and endurance. "The hardest part is being tired, and keeping a good attitude and staying motivated throughout," Widjaja said. "But by the end of it, we see teams and players coming together, learning from other shops and exchanging knowledge." Experience: Military Units: Air Force

title: Navy Advances MH-60 Modernization, Identifies Industry Performers for Prototype Project
text: Flare Deployment An MH-60R Sea Hawk assigned to Helicopter Maritime Strike Squadron 77, embarked on the aircraft carrier USS George Washington, deploys flares during a strike coordination and reconnaissance exercise while operating in the South China Sea, Aug. 12, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 788.48 KB ) Credit: Navy Seaman Anthony Vilardi VIRIN: 260812-N-VQ739-8020 In a critical step to ensure long-term fleet readiness and secure dominance in the maritime domain, the Navy's MH-60 Sea Hawk helicopter service life modernization program recently announced the industry performers identified to proceed to the first phase of a statement of work collaboration for the MH-60 tailorable architecture leveraging open systems prototype project. Led by the H-60 Multi-Mission Helicopter program office, in a joint cooperative effort with the Royal Australian Navy, the prototype project will simultaneously modernize the MH-60 avionics and mission system architecture while resolving multiple obsolescence issues. The project is designed to deliver a cost-effective platform that can rapidly respond to emerging threats, adapt to new fleet requirements and support MH-60 sustainment through the 2050 timeframe. Through collaborative digital engineering and open-system design, this joint effort strengthens U.S. and allied maritime forces' ability to outpace emerging global threats for decades to come. To execute this modernization strategy, the government is using another transaction authority agreement facilitated by the Naval Aviation Systems Consortium to engage industry partners across three critical roles: Lead aircraft integrator: Sierra Nevada Corp was identified to design the physical and structural integration for the MH-60S variant. Lockheed Martin Rotary and Mission Systems was identified to design the physical and structural integration for the MH-60R variant. Segment lead integrator-flight critical avionics segment: Rockwell Collins Inc., and Lockheed Martin Rotary and Mission Systems were identified as the segment lead integrators responsible for hardware and software architecture design, interface management, and system-level software integration for the flight critical avionics segment and the digital backbone system. Open system verification demonstration third-party integrator: Technology Security Associates Inc., was identified to support the government's assessment of how segment integrators implement a modular open systems approach in the flight critical avionics segment and the digital backbone system, including open system verification demonstrations. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} This does not constitute formal contract or agreement awards, which remain contingent upon successful negotiation and finalization of the Phase 1 statements of work, laying the groundwork for a major leap in naval aviation technology and marking a critical step toward potential prototype development for the flight critical avionics segment and the digital backbone system. Under this phased acquisition approach, Phase 1 will focus on the preliminary fight critical avionics segment and the digital backbone system design, establishing the collaborative digital engineering environment and characterizing the baseline aircraft through physical integration, structural modification, A-kit fabrication, and preparation for aircraft-level testing. Phase 2 will focus on prototype development and verification activities. By using modern digital acquisition practices and modular open systems approach standards, the prototype project will support MH-60 Sea Hawk key business drivers while also streamlining future vertical lift development with portable open core architecture. The MH-60R specializes in antisubmarine warfare, surface warfare, electronic warfare, and command and control. The MH-60S is used for performing antisurface warfare, combat search and rescue, special warfare support and airborne mine countermeasures.

title: Exercise Northern Viking Marks 75 Years of Defense Cooperation
text: U.S. service members arrived in Keflavik, Iceland, yesterday, joining forces with the Icelandic Coast Guard and other NATO allies for the U.S. 6th Fleet's Exercise Northern Viking 2026. Northern Viking Air Force Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, NATO supreme allied commander Europe and commander of U.S. European Command, delivers remarks during the opening ceremony of Exercise Northern Viking 26 at Keflavik Air Base, Iceland, Aug. 18, 2026. The exercise strengthens interoperability and force readiness between the U.S., Iceland and allied nations. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 3.25 MB ) Credit: Navy Chief Petty Officer Justin Stumberg VIRIN: 260818-N-XT273-1006 Participating nations include Belgium, Denmark, France, Iceland, Norway, Poland and the U.S., alongside specialized assets and personnel assigned to the Allied Maritime Command and NATO Joint Force Command Norfolk. "Our defense cooperation with the United States has thrived for 75 years because it has never stood still; it has developed to meet [the] evolving challenges of our time," said Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, Iceland's minister for foreign affairs, during the exercise's opening ceremony. "The best way to celebrate this anniversary is not merely by commemorating our partnership, but by actually practicing it — together and alongside our allies. Northern Viking is precisely that, a demonstration that the commitments we have made to one another are dynamic, practical and built on trust, underpinned by shared interests." This year's iteration of the biennial exercise marks the 75th anniversary of the 1951 bilateral defense agreement between Iceland and the U.S. Running from Aug. 22 to Sept. 3, Northern Viking will challenge joint and coalition forces with a series of highly realistic training scenarios. Key training opportunities will focus on antisubmarine warfare, mine countermeasures, expeditionary construction, search and rescue, humanitarian medical response and disaster response. Opening Remarks Air Force Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, NATO supreme allied commander Europe and commander of U.S. European Command, delivers remarks during the opening ceremony of Exercise Northern Viking 26 at Keflavik Air Base, Iceland, Aug. 18, 2026. Grynkewich Air Force Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, NATO supreme allied commander Europe and commander of U.S. European Command, delivers remarks during the opening ceremony of Exercise Northern Viking 26 at Keflavik Air Base, Iceland, Aug. 18, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.75 MB ) Credit: Navy Chief Petty Officer Justin Stumberg VIRIN: 260818-N-XT273-1005 "Seventy-five years of bilateral defense cooperation is a testament to the unbreakable bond between the United States and Iceland," said U.S. Navy Vice Adm. J. T. Anderson, U.S. 6th Fleet commander. "Northern Viking 2026 is a demonstration of our commitment to the collective defense of the North Atlantic. Together with our allies, we continue to create an environment that allows interoperability among NATO maritime forces so that European allies can take over primary responsibility for deterrence and defense in the European theater." Exercise Northern Viking 2026 is designed to strengthen interoperability and force readiness between the U.S., Iceland and other allied nations. The exercise enables critical multidomain command and control of joint and coalition forces defending Iceland and safeguarding the sea lines of communication within the waterways between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. As a vital global shipping corridor, keeping this area secure is an imperative for transatlantic trade, commerce and security between North America and Europe. "Together, we're honing our warfighting skills and ensuring our ability to secure this critical region and to project decisive combat power wherever and whenever necessary," said Air Force Gen Alexus G. Grynkewich, NATO supreme allied commander Europe and commander of U.S. European Command. "Throughout this exercise, and others, we will leverage the power of data in [artificial intelligence] enabled decision support tools, will integrate data streams in real time and ensure our command and control structures can make decisions at the speed of future conflict." {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} The 1951 defense agreement was the foundation of a unique security framework designating the U.S. as responsible for Iceland's defense in the absence of its own standing military. This treaty established a highly specialized and enduring defense presence in the region. Over the last 75 years, this partnership has adapted from Cold War deterrence to modern multidomain defense operations, ensuring that the transatlantic bridge remains open and secure. title: Learning With Every Launch: Inside Exercise Cold Raptor
text: After more than 50 micro-high-altitude balloon launches over the past year, a specialized team of soldiers assigned to the Multi-Domain Command – Europe learned no two flights are exactly alike, though every launch provides lessons the team can apply to the next one. Nighttime Ops Soldiers assigned to Multi-Domain Command-Europe inflate a high-altitude balloon before launch during nighttime operations in Powidz, Poland, July 28, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 122.88 KB ) Credit: Army Sgt. 1st Class Rajheem Dixon VIRIN: 260731-A-IU004-9741 The team recently conducted a week of balloon launches in Poland during Exercise Cold Raptor. The training supported NATO 's Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, a NATO-led regional initiative supported by U.S. Army Europe and Africa that integrates emerging technologies to strengthen deterrence and readiness along NATO's eastern flank. Cold Raptor gave soldiers hands-on experience launching, tracking and operating tactical balloons in a European environment while refining the procedures they will use during future missions. Decentralized Operations and Multidomain Readiness Soldiers assigned to the Extended Range Sensing and Effects Company, 2nd Multi-Domain Effects Battalion, conducted the training. Many on the team are qualified satellite communication systems operator-maintainers and are applying their signal expertise to emerging high-altitude systems. Army Sgt. Eric Atwater Jr., a signal sergeant, said the exercise tested the team's ability to operate from separate locations. "The purpose of Cold Raptor was to see how our launch team and our pilot team can operate from decentralized points," Atwater said. "We wanted to maintain communications while balloons go up in one location, while the flight trajectory is managed and monitored by another team off-site." For Army Sgt. Shakir Claxton, a fellow high-altitude balloon operator, improvement comes from repetition. "The biggest thing is getting us out in the field, setting everything up, making sure we have a solid timeframe we can work within and doing as many launches as we can," Claxton said. "The more repetitions we get, the better we get at the job." Training Time U.S. Army and Polish soldiers recover a high-altitude balloon payload in Powidz, Poland, July 28, 2026. The combined recovery operation strengthened interoperability and demonstrated the allies' ability to coordinate high-altitude operations across the European theater. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 235.52 KB ) Credit: Army Sgt. 1st Class Rajheem Dixon VIRIN: 260731-A-IU004-8799 The training also supported the company's broader multidomain mission. Claxton compared their capabilities to the three prongs of a trident, each contributing to the sensing mission. "We put up the balloons to give a certain kind of view of an area, while other parts of our company, like [unmanned aircraft systems] and [electronic warfare], work hand in hand on the sensing aspect," he said. Adapting to Changing Conditions During the exercise, the team conducted launches from Powidz, Poland. Some of the balloons ascended into the stratosphere, reaching altitudes between 60,000 and 70,000 feet — approximately 18,300 to 21,400 meters — while carrying experimental payloads designed to extend communications and improve domain awareness. Operating in the stratosphere requires precision. Teams must account for changing weather conditions while meeting strict aviation schedules. "We have specific windows when these balloons need to go up to meet mission requirements," Atwater said. "Whenever we're contacting airspace control, they're expecting these terminals to be in the air at specific times. If something goes wrong, you have to think quickly on your feet, troubleshoot and find the cause in a timely manner." Micro-high-altitude balloon technology continues to evolve and operating the experimental equipment throughout the week presented the team with real-world challenges. By troubleshooting problems as they occurred, soldiers successfully completed flights throughout the exercise and collected data to support continued experimentation. The lessons learned during Exercise Cold Raptor also contribute to a broader effort to strengthen deterrence along NATO's eastern flank. The Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative is not a single unit or location, but a distributed system of capabilities operating across domains and nations. The concept aligns land forces with NATO's regional defense plans and connects mission command systems, networks and data so allied forces can share a common operating picture and make decisions faster. Exercises like this help determine how emerging technologies can contribute to the larger effort. Nighttime Ops Soldiers assigned to Multi-Domain Command-Europe control a high-altitude balloon as it inflates before launch during nighttime operations in Powidz, Poland, July 28, 2026. The operation tested the unit's ability to prepare and employ high-altitude capabilities under field conditions. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 204.8 KB ) Credit: Army Sgt. 1st Class Rajheem Dixon VIRIN: 260731-A-IU004-9589 "The Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative operationalizes all-domain deterrence for NATO through a data-enabled posture that harnesses the changes in the character of war," said Army Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter, commanding general of Multi-Domain Command – Europe. "Experimentation with emerging technologies allows us to better understand the operational environment, refine how we integrate capabilities across domains and strengthen our ability to deter aggression alongside our NATO allies." Allied Interoperability and Airspace Coordination Launching from Poland required more than preparing the balloons and monitoring their flights. The team also coordinated closely with Polish authorities to ensure each launch met host nation airspace requirements. "Airspace coordination is a major priority with this kind of mission," Claxton said. "We have an excellent communication pipeline and a strong working relationship with our Polish partners." That coordination extended to the flight line, where the launches drew interest from Polish partner forces. Because Polish forces had not previously worked with this type of platform in Poland, U.S. soldiers provided hands-on demonstrations of the equipment and launch process. The demonstrations allowed Polish soldiers to see the technology up close and build a shared understanding of the capability. For the soldiers on the ground, helping develop the emerging capability carries responsibility and opportunity. "Initially trained as a 25 Sierra [satellite communication systems operator-maintainer], the Army already entrusted me to support established communications equipment," Atwater said. "Being introduced to something new and experimental is an honor. What feels like growing pains for us right now will end up being the foundation that future soldiers rely on." For him, the mission also connects to a childhood dream. "When I was a kid, I wanted to be an astronaut," Atwater said. "What I would say to my younger self is: you might not be the one going up to the stars, but you'll be the reason everyone looks to the sky and knows you sent something up to the very edge of space. They'll feel safer knowing you put it there." Spotlight: NATO Spotlight: Science and Technology Spotlight: Engineering in DOW Spotlight: DOW Innovates

title: United Nations Command Pays Tribute to Fallen Soldiers During 50th Commemoration of Attack
text: Fifty years ago today, Army Capt. Arthur Bonifas and Army 1st Lt. Mark Barrett set out to trim a large poplar tree that blocked visibility between a United Nations Command checkpoint and an observation post at the joint security area in the Korean Demilitarized Zone. Memorial Salute Family members of Army Maj. Arthur G. Bonifas and Army 1st Lt. Mark T. Barrett attend the 50th commemoration honoring the soldiers at Camp Bonifas, South Korea, Aug. 18, 2026. The ceremony commemorated the two Army officers who were killed by North Korean guards in 1976 while leading a work party to trim a tree in the Korean Demilitarized Zone. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.41 MB ) Credit: Stacey Yun, Army VIRIN: 260818-A-HL290-1351 Although operating in the security area between North and South Korea always carried risks, trimming the tree was routine. However, about 30 North Korean guards rushed the soldiers, who were leading a work party to prune the tree, violently killing them in an unprovoked attack. In response to the attack, the U.S. and South Korea conducted Operation Paul Bunyan three days later to cut down the tree. The mission included 16 military engineers, 124 ground troops, 27 aircraft and several field artillery teams, making it the largest demonstration of force since the 1953 Korean Armistice Agreement. Every year since, the United Nations Command commemorates the tragic incident by remembering the sacrifice of Bonifas, posthumously promoted to major, and Barrett in the name of peace and stability. A memorial to them now stands atop the tree stump near a bridge in the security area. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} This year, for the 50th commemoration, Bonifas' grandchildren, Brady and Dylan, offered touching remarks at the memorial about how they got to know their grandfather through his letters. "We learned that Arthur Bonifas cared deeply about the soldiers with whom he served and the people entrusted to his leadership," Brady said. "Through these letters, we came to know our grandfather not only as a soldier and a leader, but also as a husband, a father and a man guided by love," Dylan said. "We are also grateful to everyone who has continued to preserve his memory and honor his service and sacrifice." Remembering Sacrifice Australian Army Lt. Gen. Scott Winter, United Nations Command deputy commander, U.S. Army Command Sgt. Maj. Robin Bolmer, United Nations Command senior enlisted leader, along with family members of Army Maj. Arthur G. Bonifas and Army 1st Lt. Mark T. Barrett, pose for a group photo during the 50th commemoration honoring Bonifas and Barrett at Camp Bonifas, South Korea, Aug. 18, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.76 MB ) Credit: Army Sgt. Seongho Park VIRIN: 260818-A-XO140-5849 Fiftieth Commemoration Australian Army Lt. Gen. Scott Winter, United Nations Command deputy commander, greets family members of Army Maj. Arthur G. Bonifas during the 50th commemoration honoring Bonifas and Army 1st Lt. Mark T. Barrett at Camp Bonifas, South Korea, Aug. 18, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.19 MB ) Credit: Army Sgt. Seongho Park VIRIN: 260818-A-XO140-5760 During the ceremony, Stacy Adams, Barrett's niece, also reflected on her uncle's voluntary service, military unity and loss. "When conflicts required their presence, our military performed expertly and professionally," Adams said. "Yet sometimes the well-coordinated force lost a member. One fell from the many. The many knew to fill the vacuum, to cover for each other, to have each other's back, but they felt the loss of the one." Bonifas and Barrett operated on the most front line of freedom in South Korea, and 50 years later, the United Nations Command's security battalion there continues the mission to secure the critical location with the same courage and under the same flag.

title: Hegseth Touts Americas Counter Cartel Coalition During Panama Visit
text: In Panama today, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth told members of the recently established Americas Counter Cartel Coalition that the U.S. is firmly committed to working alongside them to dismantle dangerous transnational criminal drug cartels. Panama Arrival Secretary of War Pete Hegseth arrives in Panama, Aug. 12, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1013.76 KB ) Credit: DOW VIRIN: 260812-D-D0439-9001 Launched in March by President Donald J. Trump, the coalition — sometimes called "Shield of the Americas" — is a U.S.-led multinational security and political alliance formed to combat transnational drug cartels, reduce illegal migration across the Western Hemisphere and limit foreign geopolitical interference. "I'm grateful to be here with ministers and chiefs of defense, united in purpose and resolve, as partners in the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition," Hegseth said. "Just a few months ago, we laid out a shared vision for a safe, secure Western Hemisphere, where borders and laws are respected, and narco-terrorists are brought to swift and absolute justice." Over the last two days, 19 partner members of the A3C met in Panama for a coalition-wide discussion. Marine Corps Gen. Francis L. Donovan, commander of U.S. Southern Command, said A3C members share a common understanding of the threat posed by criminal networks operating in the hemisphere. "Coalition campaigning creates systemic friction on these networks," he said. "Our strength is in our complementary capabilities. Persistence and unity will drive scale and will drive victory." During the meetings, Donovan said, next steps were decided, which included refining priority network campaign plans, designating roles and lead nations, establishing working groups with specific objectives and milestones, and initiating coalition campaign assessments. Americas Counter Cartel Coalition Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met with Colombian military leaders, including Colombia Minister of National Defense Jorge Mora, in Panama City, Aug. 12, 2026. During the meetings, Colombia joined the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 399.36 KB ) Credit: Department of War VIRIN: 260812-D-DO439-1001 "Between now and November, we are going to write an A3C campaign plan," he said. "We will staff it with our teammates and our members here in the room, and we'll approve it by November." The general also said coalition nations are eager to volunteer to lead in areas important to them. "Yesterday, by the end of our session, we went out and made the initial pulse … who wants to lead in different regions? Who wants to lead to … go after these networks?" Donovan said. "We had volunteers right away, nations that wanted to step forward and take [the] lead in subregions and go after certain threats." The United States, Hegseth said, is committed to dismantling the drug cartels that threaten safety, security and sovereignty in the Western Hemisphere. "When we say we will dismantle the cartels, we mean it, and I know the nations of this coalition feel the exact same way ... and will take concrete steps — sometimes risky steps, courageous steps — in partnership." The citizens of the U.S., of coalition partner nations, and of the entire Western Hemisphere, Hegseth said, deserve and expect real, concrete actions. Americas Counter Cartel Coalition Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno and Colombia's Minister of National Defense Jorge Mora pose with signed copies of an agreement bringing Colombia into the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition in Panama City, Aug. 12, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 317.44 KB ) Credit: Department of War VIRIN: 260812-D-DO439-1002 "We believe there's no time to waste and no better time than right now," he said. "We will be with you, I pledge to you, from the White House to the Pentagon, shoulder to shoulder, every step of the way." The nations in the coalition are united by heritage, history, faith, geography, and a shared interest in security and prosperity, Hegseth said, adding that narco-terrorism threatens all of that. "I want to thank each and every one of you for supporting our ability to find, fix and finish narco-terrorist targets," he said." As head of the A3C, the secretary also announced an update for the coalition. "The new motto of the A3C is 'We do bad things to bad people,'" he said. "That's the mentality I want to have inside this room. ... We're dealing with bad people that have done a lot of bad things to a lot of good people, for a very long time. And they're about to meet a new sheriff in town in the A3C. And we mean business. Narco-terrorists … drug traffickers are hereby on notice. Under President Trump, we will make the Americas great again. The safety and prosperity of one will strengthen the safety and prosperity of all." During his visit to Panama, the secretary met with Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino and also has plans to meet with U.S. service members at the jungle operations training course and observe Panamax training events. title: Southcom Mission Shifts to Protecting Sovereignty of U.S., Partner Nations
text: At the Combined Jungle Training Center-South in Cristobal Colon, Panama, yesterday, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met with U.S. service members who are learning how to survive in the most brutal, unforgiving jungles of the Western Hemisphere, all while retaining their combat effectiveness. Troop Meeting Secretary of War Pete Hegseth meets with U.S. service members at the Jungle Operations Training Center-South in Panama, Aug. 12, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.28 MB ) Credit: DOW VIRIN: 260812-D-DO439-8001 The visit coincided with the secretary's address during the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, a U.S.-led multinational security and political alliance formed to combat transnational drug cartels, reduce illegal migration across the Western Hemisphere and limit foreign geopolitical interference. It also coincided with Exercise Panamax 2026 , a multinational military exercise hosted by Panama and sponsored by U.S. Southern Command. In the dense jungle on the northern side of the Panama Canal, Hegseth told service members at the training center that what they are doing is exactly what he likes to see when he meets with warfighters. "I think this is what ... the warrior ethos looks like; it's what reestablishing it looks like," he said. "It happens in training centers like this, with Americans like this, who do really difficult things in really tough places." While at the training center, Hegseth met with instructors assigned to the Jungle Operations Training Course-Panama, along with Marines assigned to Littoral Combat Force-24, who were in Panama to participate in Panamax. Panamax Meeting Service members train at the Jungle Operations Training Center-South in Panama, Aug. 12, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.86 MB ) Credit: DOW VIRIN: 260812-D-DO439-8002 Jungle Training Secretary of War Pete Hegseth observes service members training at the Jungle Operations Training Center-South in Panama, Aug. 12, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.28 MB ) Credit: DOW VIRIN: 260812-D-DO439-8003 The secretary said the service members who train at the center are willing to do things no other Americans are willing to do, to include helping U.S. allies in both Central and South America protect the nation's backyard. "That's what we're doing here with the A3C [and with] Panamax ... expanding peace through strength in our hemisphere, right here in the jungles with our partners," he said. Noting a big shift in the Southcom mission, Hegseth said that just 18 months ago, the command was less focused on protecting the Americas and deterring threats. The Jungle Operations Training Center in Panama is exactly how we re-establish deterrence. Real capabilities. Real training. Real readiness. pic.twitter.com/uizQkoY8Ex — Sean Parnell (@SeanParnellASW) August 13, 2026 "This is a different Southcom; this is a different mission," he said. "We are focused on military capabilities against real threats who need to be deterred and defeated, and we're going to give them everything they need to do it, on behalf of the American people." The secretary said that under President Donald J. Trump, Southcom's mission has focused on working with partners in the region to keep everybody safe from a variety of shared threats. "We know exactly what that mission looks like," he said. "We're empowering commanders like [Marine Corps Gen. Francis L. Donovan] to do it in Southcom; we're working with partners like Panama, like Ecuador, like Colombia ... they're going to send students here soon to swim across this very same river, [to] be a part of this very same training." The nations involved in the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition — 19 nations in all, with Colombia signing on just yesterday — are going to be involved in the same training as U.S. service members in Panama. The secretary said that the same things that necessitate American jungle training also motivate every other nation in the region. "It turns out, in the [Western] Hemisphere, they face the very same security challenges, the same threat of drugs, the same threat of criminal cartels that threaten their citizens, the same ones that threaten our citizens," Hegseth said. U.S. law enforcement personnel stationed at the U.S. southern border to stop illegal immigration and drug traffickers, combined with training across Central and South America in places such as Ecuador, Colombia and Panama, puts increasing pressure on shared threats. "That's going after the enemies of our country — designated terrorist organizations — unabashedly," Hegseth said. Earlier in the day, the secretary announced the new motto of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition: "We do bad things to bad people." "For too long, bad people did bad things to good people, inside the United States of America and across Central and South America," he said. "We're going to empower great Americans and great partners to do really good stuff and be very capable about bringing violence against drug cartels and designated terrorist organizations, because we're dead serious about securing the homeland." {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} A big part of that is the Trump corollary to the Monroe Doctrine. In 1823, President James Monroe articulated a foreign policy, now known as the Monroe Doctrine, which declared that the Western Hemisphere was off-limits to further colonization efforts or interference by European nations. Later, that expanded to include interference by any foreign power. In 1904, President Theodore Roosevelt added to that doctrine that the U.S. could intervene in the affairs of Latin America to protect U.S. interests. And now, Hegseth said, there is Trump's corollary to the Monroe Doctrine. "It is a recognition that [designated terrorist organizations] ... will not control our hemisphere ... and we will not allow foreign malign influence to take over ... key terrain like the Panama Canal," he said. Hegseth said Colombia's inclusion in the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition is significant. "The A3C had formed, but in some ways, it missed part of its core," he said. "Colombia is going to be [an] incredible partner. They offered to be a headquarters or a hub for the A3C as the brand-new 19th member. They've got ... hundreds of thousands of capable members of their military and decades of training with the United States ... that mil-to-mil relationship has been long-standing, and that's why they're coming to this jungle course soon." title: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth Remarks at Joint Base Lindsey Graham Naming Ceremony (As Delivered)
text: SECRETARY OF WAR PETE HEGSETH: Well, Senator, Governor, Mr. Secretary, thank you for hitching a ride with us this morning to sunny South Carolina. All patriots I've had a chance to work with, our great Treasury Secretary, and he is a patriot of the highest order and loves our military, so it's an honor to have you here today. Senator Lindsey Graham dedicated his life to serving this state and serving the Armed forces of the United States. He served this nation both in uniform and in both houses of Congress, as everyone here knows. But in both capacities, it was always the same mission. He knew the timeless truth that to ensure peace, we must be prepared for war. Protect your people, protect your state, protect your sovereignty, or you will lose it to someone else who is willing to take it from you. Lindsey spent his final years taking on a radical leftist ideology that had run rampant in the media, in academia, and even among a few members of Congress. The hard left declared war on our own military. This nation spent 45 years fighting communism in the Cold War, and that was 30 years ago. Now it seems that many people have forgotten the reality of what communism looks like. It starts off with promises and it ends in prisons. It promises heaven but delivers hell. Senator Graham stood up against that radical woke ideology that killed our military recruiting. Under the previous administration, they couldn't even hit recruiting goals. Young patriots didn't want to serve under these woke so-called “leaders.” But instead of raising standards, they lowered goals. President Trump promised the American people, alongside Senator Graham, that he would rebuild the military. He promised he would make our forces stronger than ever, and that he would run those radicals out of the Pentagon, and that's exactly what he and we have done. In this new golden age of America, President Trump has had no stronger ally in Congress than Colonel Lindsey Graham. It falls to us to complete the work that Lindsey Graham began and advocated for, for decades. As we gather here today, the War Department is seeking a historic generational investment of $1.5 trillion for American warriors. And Lindsey himself said, to me in his office, “this is the best military budget I've seen since I've been in Congress” – end quote. This department pays tribute to Lindsey Graham in the naming of this base, but there could be no greater tribute than Congress could give than to invest in our warriors for the full $1.5 trillion. More on that in a moment. Fully funding our warriors would be one last great accomplishment for Colonel Lindsey Graham and a major part of his legacy. And I believe that he will continue here and around the world to inspire airmen for generations to come. And I say around the world, because, as was mentioned, those gray tails that say Charleston, now, when they land in far flung places, will say, Graham. The world will remember that name. South Carolinians grow up with stories of legendary warriors from this state, warriors like the swamp fox, Francis Marion, who helped win our freedom at Yorktown; like Lieutenant Irwin David Shaw, a pilot who gave his life in World War I; or General Bernie McIntyre, who spent his final moments saving innocent lives; or how about just a few weeks ago, President Trump gave the Medal of Honor to a marine who fought the communists in the jungles of Vietnam, James Capers, Jr. of Lee County, South Carolina. Now, South Carolinians will grow up learning about the namesake of this incredible joint base, Senator Lindsey Graham. I'm proud to say that I actually knew him for more than 20 years. I was telling his sister that. Nineteen years ago, young lieutenant, uh, First Lieutenant Pete Hegseth came back from Iraq and was a part of a veterans' organization called Vets for Freedom that believed in the surge in Iraq and advocating for the troops on the ground. We were a young, scrappy veterans' organization with no money and no access and connections. The first and only senator willing to meet with First Lieutenant Pete Hegseth and nowheresville Vets for Freedom, was Senator Lindsey Graham. He welcomed us into his conference room, sat us down as a bunch of lieutenants and NCOs and others around the table, fresh back from Iraq, who wanted the right strategy. I'll never forget it in his accent, he sat there and he said, gentlemen -- I can't do it. It always devolves into a Trump accent. He said, gentlemen, welcome to a place where you can still say the word victory. He believed in mission success. He believed in the troops. He believed in giving the troops everything they needed. And he served himself. In fact, a few years later, Captain Hegseth was an instructor in a base on the outskirts of Kabul in Afghanistan and who came to visit, Colonel Lindsey Graham. I had mentioned that we were out there at the counterinsurgency school, and we could give him an update on what the Taliban was up to. Sure enough, during his reserve duty, there he was, jet-lagged as all -- as all hell, because man had a schedule like nobody else. But he was there to hear from us because he wanted his ear to the ground for the truth of what was actually happening in the war in Afghanistan. Fast forward, I mentioned the military budget of $1.5 trillion. The last meeting I had with Senator Graham was about a week before his passing, uh, or so, maybe two weeks before his passing. And he said, uh, he's the budget committee chairman, so, Mr. Secretary, what do you need for a reconciliation? I said, well, in total, sir, we're going to need $350 billion for our military. That's what we believe gets us to 1.5 trillion – $115 billion in the base budget, $350 billion in reconciliation and we'll be ready. He looked at me and said, how's $355 billion sound? He wanted to give even more than $350 billion. He wanted to ensure our military was as equipped as humanly possible, because he was thinking of places like this one right here. I saw firsthand as a young first lieutenant, as a captain in a combat zone, and as a secretary, the unwavering commitment of Lindsey Graham. And he knew that if you're going to seek peace, you have to be prepared for war. You have to have a prepared military. If you walk -- talk the talk and walk the walk. And now, 20 years later, thanks to his help in the Senate, this administration is breaking recruiting records for beating our goals. We're taking back the department from the wokesters, and we're making sure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon. Every president for a quarter century declared that they would not let Iran get a nuclear weapon, but they never did anything about it, until President Donald J. Trump. And Lindsey Graham was right there for him in the Senate. And so now it falls to us to continue Senator Graham's work of building up our military, the hard work of defending this nation. And I know with full confidence, that is exactly what we will do. Well done, Colonel Graham. We have the watch from here. So my fellow Americans, it is my honor to say welcome to Joint Base Lindsey Graham. May God bless you.

title: Hegseth Renames Joint Base Charleston to Honor Late Sen. Lindsey Graham
text: Joint Base Charleston, South Carolina, became Joint Base Lindsey Graham during a ceremony today to rename the installation after the late senator, Air Force veteran and South Carolina native son. Joint Base Lindsey Graham Left to right: Scott Bessent, treasury secretary; Secretary of War Pete Hegseth; Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina; and South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster pose for a photo following a ceremony to rename Joint Base Charleston, S.C., as Joint Base Lindsey Graham, Aug. 10, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 3.99 MB ) Credit: Army Sgt. 1st Class Curt Loter VIRIN: 260810-A-GL508-9001 Secretary of War Pete Hegseth joined South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster and Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina to dedicate the 32-square-mile installation, home to the 437th Airlift Wing, which provides global airlift capability to the joint force with the C-17A Globemaster III aircraft. Lindsey Graham served as a U.S. senator from South Carolina from January 2003 until his passing July 11. He also served as a lawyer and commissioned officer in the Air Force's Judge Advocate General Corps, first on active duty from 1982 until 1988, then as a member of the South Carolina Air National Guard until 1995 and finally, in the Air Force Reserve until 2015. "Sen. Lindsey Graham dedicated his life to serving this state and serving the armed forces of the United States," Hegseth said. "He served this nation both in uniform and in both houses of Congress. ... But in both capacities, it was always the same mission. He knew the timeless truth that to ensure peace, we must be prepared for war. Protect your people, protect your state, protect your sovereignty, or you will lose it to someone else who is willing to take it from you." Hegseth said he first met Graham as a young first lieutenant in the Army. Hegseth had returned from Iraq and had aligned himself with a veterans group called "Vets for Freedom." "[We] believed in the surge in Iraq and advocating for the troops on the ground," he said. "We were a young, scrappy veterans' organization with no money and no access and connections." Only one senator, Graham, was willing to meet with Hegseth and other representatives of the group. 20:47 "He welcomed us into his conference room, sat us down as a bunch of lieutenants and [noncommissioned officers] and others around the table — fresh back from Iraq — who wanted the right strategy," Hegseth said. "He said, 'Gentlemen, welcome to a place where you can still say the word victory.' He believed in mission success; he believed in the troops; he believed in giving the troops everything they needed." In later years, Hegseth said he recalled mentioning to Graham that he was now serving as an instructor at a counterinsurgency school in Kabul, Afghanistan. "I had mentioned that we ... could give him an update on what the Taliban was up to," he said. "Sure enough, during his reserve duty, there he was — jet-lagged as all hell — because that man had a schedule like nobody else. But he was there to hear from us because he wanted his ear to the ground from the troops on what was actually happening in the war in Afghanistan." Just weeks before the senator's passing, Hegseth said he met with Graham to discuss the War Department budget — the current request, $1.5 trillion, is the largest in U.S. history. The senator showed his commitment to troops there, too. "[He asked], 'Mr. Secretary, what do you need for reconciliation?'" Hegseth said. Hegseth said he discussed with Graham that he thought the department needed $1.15 trillion in the base budget and $350 billion in reconciliation to get to the needed $1.5 trillion total budget. "He looked at me and said, 'How's $355 billion sound to you?'" Hegseth said. "He wanted to give even more than $350 [billion]. He wanted to ensure our military was as equipped as humanly possible, because he was thinking of places like this one right here." Graham, Hegseth said, knew what was needed to keep America safe. "I saw firsthand as a young first lieutenant, as a captain in a combat zone and as a secretary, the unwavering commitment of Lindsey Graham," Hegseth said. "He knew that if you're going to seek peace, you have to be prepared for war. You have to have a prepared military. He talked the talk, and he walked the walk." Darline Graham took on his role as senator following her brother's passing. She said he was proud of his service in the Air Force. "What an honor for my brother, and what a tribute to his 33 years of service," Graham said. "Lindsey loved the Air Force. He loved its mission. He loved wearing the uniform of his country. His interest in foreign affairs and national security started with his service in the Air Force." Lindsey Graham initially served in state government as a member of the South Carolina House of Representatives. Later, from 1995 to 2003, he served in the U.S. House of Representatives, representing South Carolina's 2nd District. And finally, he served as a U.S. senator from South Carolina, beginning in 2003. "It was sometimes hard to tell if Lindsey was a senator who happened to serve in the Air Force or an Air Force lawyer who happened to serve in the Senate," his sister said. "Such was his love for both. That's the man this base is named after — a man who loved his country, loved his state and loved the United States Air Force. I could not be more honored or humbled for him to be recognized in such a fashion for his lifetime of service." Following the renaming of the installation, Hegseth met with airmen assigned to the 437th Airlift Wing as well as other troops on the installation who had been involved with Operation Epic Fury, the mission to destroy Iranian offensive missiles and missile production, as well as the Iranian navy and other security infrastructure. {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} - {{slideCaption}} Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( {{filesize}} ) Credit: {{photographer}} VIRIN: {{virin}} {{slideNumber}} of {{numSlides}} {{slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideTitle}} - {{slideCaption}} {{slideInfo.slideNumber}}/{{numSlides}} {{slideInfo.slideTitle}} - {{slideInfo.slideCaption}} While meeting with airmen, the secretary discussed the importance of logistics. He commended them on their improvements to logistics capabilities and how their unit is contributing to the modernization of the U.S. military. "Look at what the 437th is doing as the premier maneuver force for the C-17A modernization: leading operational testing for things like palletized munitions, drastically increasing our airborne munitions capacity in future conflicts," he said. "I've been watching. I read the reports of how you iterate, do things faster in congested logistics. It's incredible, the backbone of what you have enabled in the theater." Logistics, Hegseth said, is how wars are won, adding that it's airmen at Joint Base Lindsey Graham who are making that happen. 17:45 "The secret sauce of any successful mission — whether it's Epic Fury, Southern Spear, Midnight Hammer, Absolute Resolve, Hawkeye Strike, you name it — are the logistics behind it," he said. "That's the genius of the United States military." The secretary said it's the strategic lift, the U.S. Transportation Command, logistics, how the U.S. moves things, people, munitions and capabilities that make a difference. "No one else can touch it, not even close," Hegseth said, adding that, "All of it is enabled by all of you, incredible Americans at the top of your game, at the prime of your life. ... I consider all of you the real 1%, the real elite who give absolutely everything."
