title: Remarks by Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby at the Stratbase Institute in Manila, Philippines (As Prepared)
text: Thank you for that generous introduction. This is my first official trip to Southeast Asia as Under Secretary of War for Policy. Starting here in Manila is deeply fitting. The Philippines is our oldest mutual defense treaty ally in Asia, and we share a deep and abiding historical connection in addition to our profound alignment of strategic interest. From Manila, I will be traveling onward to Jakarta, Bangkok, and Phnom Penh. As in Manila, I intend to deliver a clear message that is at once both realistic and perhaps bracing but also reassuring: That America's interests are more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific, and that we at the Department of War are concentrated on ensuring those interests are stoutly defended. This means a strong and growing U.S. investment in the region. But it is also coupled with a newfound but common sense expectation of much greater effort and contribution by our allies and partners. Not in a hectoring or unbalanced way. To the contrary, in a spirit of partnership, not dependency; of realism, not idle cloud-castle abstraction; of respect, not patronization. Our approach, as laid out in the Administration's National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy and set out eloquently by Secretary Hegseth in his Shangri-La speeches this year and last, is straightforward. Our legacy foreign policy of the post-Cold War period was fundamentally out of date and ill-advised. In the years following the collapse of the Soviet Union, American strategy was characterized by high-flown abstractions and comfortable illusions of permanent unipolarity. Washington's strategic approach became unmoored from the concrete realities of power, geography, economics, and limits. Our foreign policy became detached from clear-headed strategic rationality, and the results were demonstrably poor. President Trump has reversed that failed course. Under Secretary Hegseth's leadership at the Pentagon, we are carrying out the President's agenda to restore American strength, put Americans' concrete interests first, and do so in a way that updates our relationships around the world and puts them on a much sounder footing. As we see it, President Trump's approach to foreign policy is one of common sense. Accordingly, he is recalibrating America's foreign policy to serve the practical, concrete interests of regular Americans, with significant implications from defense to trade to counternarcotics to migration. To be clear, this is not some dramatic abandonment of America's historic foreign policy. Actually quite to the contrary: It is a return to the best tradition of America's foreign policy — of a hard-nosed, clear-eyed republican realism that puts our people's concrete interests first, but in ways that also align with the interests of many other countries. It is not isolation, but rather a business-like recalibration, a model of collaborative self-interest — enlightened self-interest, yes, but very much practical and pragmatic rather than ideological or rigid. In Europe, we talk about this as NATO 3.0 — a rejection of the fanciful era of post-Cold War talking shop NATO and a return to the tradition of the hard-nosed Atlantic Alliance of the Cold War period, focused on the core business of military strength and readiness. In the Western Hemisphere, meanwhile, we see the Trump Corollary as a return to the best tradition of the Monroe Doctrine — of a policy designed to empower and enable the countries of Latin America to deal with the serious challenges we together face in the Western Hemisphere. In both of these regions, despite a lot of sniping in the outlets of the old order, we see real, concrete, and accelerating momentum to join us in building new, more pragmatic, and more durable partnerships with our allies and partners. NATO is demonstrably much stronger than it was before President Trump's leadership. And in the Western Hemisphere countries across the region are joining us in efforts like the America's Counter-Cartel Coalition initiative to combat the scourge of narcoterrorism that afflicts us all. We see similar trends here in Asia. Countries in the region know that we are not embarking on some novel approach of retrenchment. That is the cheap talk of the cognoscenti. Instead, countries here in Asia understand that America is returning to a traditional, time-tested strategy of flexible realism: clarity about our priorities, seriousness about deterrence, and an understanding of the value of both forcefulness and diplomacy. It is the foreign policy of common sense. Viewing the world through this lens, we see Asia as of paramount importance. The National Security Strategy states, in plain terms, that in order "to thrive at home, we must successfully compete" here. The National Defense Strategy, meantime, lays out that maintaining U.S. access to this critical region has "exceptionally real — indeed, fundamental — implications" for America's vital interests. And, as Secretary Hegseth said at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, "a Pacific dominated by any hegemon would unravel the regional balance of power and undermine the equilibrium we all seek to preserve." This longstanding view of the United States — an Asia free of hegemony — has been at the core of our regional approach since the earliest days of our Republic. America's interests here in the Indo-Pacific region are therefore clear, abiding, and profound. Not in some vague way. But in the concrete, practical sense that this region will be the world's largest market. It is where not only scale is, but growth as well, including especially here in ASEAN. This is not a new observation. Indeed, this recognition of the importance of Asia is also a return to the deep roots of American foreign policy. Such an understanding of the rising importance of Asia and its economic heft goes back not only to the postwar period but to the 19th century — to the Open Door, the opening of Japan, and of course America's presence here in the Philippines as well as across the Pacific in places like Hawaii and Samoa. In light of these factors, as the NSS says, our driving and abiding purpose is to maintain a favorable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific. From a defense perspective, as that seminal document makes clear, this requires us to maintain a posture of deterrence by denial along the first island chain. As Secretary Hegseth put it at the 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue, "We will build and sustain a strong denial defense in the Western Pacific that ensures aggression is infeasible, escalation unattractive, and war deemed irrational." This is what we at the Pentagon are focused on building and sustaining here in this region. And the results and progress are clear, not only in our operations and activities, but in the unprecedented degree of investment reflected in the Administration's Fiscal Year 2027 defense budget. But, to be clear, this strong and focused approach is fully consistent with an active and creative diplomacy aimed at promoting strategic stability and reducing pressures toward conflict. To many today in Washington and the elite commentariat, this seems hard to wrap their heads around. But it is simple common sense, and indeed in the best traditions of American foreign policy. Dwight Eisenhower, Richard Nixon and Henry Kissinger, and, yes, Ronald Reagan all both sought to strengthen America's military position while simultaneously engaging actively at the highest levels with our potential opponents. As Winston Churchill himself put it, "it is better to jaw jaw than war war." Indeed, this is much closer to the ASEAN way than Washington's foreign policy of the last generation. Our understanding of the ASEAN way is that it is defined by pragmatism, an openness to dialogue, respect for counterparts, proud nationalism, and a focus on economic prosperity. The United States is now taking a page from the ASEAN Way. These are also the key themes of President Trump's administration. This is not an approach that purports to stand in judgment of every action by other countries, as has been so typical of the post-Cold War American approach here in the region. We will of course stick to and stand for our principles, but we will not hold hostage progress on key issues of strategic importance because of them. The concrete, practical progress with many countries here in ASEAN over the last eighteen months shows that. We may not agree on everything, but we respect your countries, your independent pathways, your nationalism, and the reality of our shared interests to work together collaboratively wherever we can. In summary, then, our approach is one of flexible realism, of building strength in ways that are durable and achieve their intended effect, of genuine peace through strength rather than rhetorical pressurization without adequate material strength and resolve. In other words, strong and clear but quiet, as Secretary Hegseth puts it: not peacocking but the intelligent, realistic, and quiet development and demonstration of strength. Now, I acknowledge that this is a different reality than what you might hear if you confine yourself to listening only to the panjandrums of the global elite or their most prominent outlets. There, you will read or hear a different story: that America is in retreat or decline or too unreliable, and that Asian countries are fleeing from working with us. The commentariat plays an important role and often makes valuable points. But they are missing the reality of the situation — perhaps not seeing it, and in some cases perhaps not wishing to admit to seeing it. Governments in the region, though, do not have this luxury. For them and for those in the commentariat who wish seriously to help governments here understand what is happening, I humbly advise looking at the reality of the situation. If you do this, you will quickly observe a far different reality than what is commonly presented. First, America is decidedly not in decline. Our economy under President Trump's leadership is growing, and indeed substantially outgrowing the other OECD economies. Our technology remains at the world's forefront, and in key respects we are extending our lead. In fact, it now seems increasingly likely that America will remain the largest economy in nominal GDP terms for the foreseeable future — something that would not have been so clear a decade ago. Second, America is definitely not disengaging from Asia — to the contrary. Our vital national interests dictate our enduring presence here. What the commentariat frequently misinterprets as "disengagement" or "retrenchment" is, in reality, a disciplined and necessary strategic prioritization. We are replacing the hollow, merely symbolic engagement of previous decades with a formidable, resource-backed posture calibrated to actual structural realities. We are not leaving; in fact, we are digging in, to ensure a favorable balance of power where it matters most. Third, contrary to the hubbub, you most definitely can cooperate with America — in fact, there are new vistas opening up to do so. But the terms of engagement have changed. Allow me to try to explain this. There is a canard out there that America today is too unreliable to work with anymore. That is a combination of wrong and missing the point. Before, America was at the same time calculable from a negotiating point of view but frequently rigid and ideologically fixed on liberal shibboleths. Under President Trump's visionary leadership, we have a new approach defined by common sense. It is true that America now drives a harder bargain. But that is downstream of republican realism oriented on actually putting Americans first. Under President Trump's leadership, the simple fact is that countries can no longer take America for granted. No longer can countries simply assume America will go along with unbalanced relationships that are not clearly in Americans' practical interests. We are proud to implement that in the defense arena, where this has very clear and direct implications in terms of pressing allies to spend more on defense, for instance. But saying countries can no longer take America for granted is definitely not the same thing as saying we cannot be dealt with. To the contrary. Rather, if you approach as we approach you — with a practical mindset, focused on delivering results that reflect a reasonable balance in the relationship — you will find us willing partners, and indeed more willing than past administrations, which were hidebound by outdated convention or rigid adherence to liberal dogma. Moreover, the reality that is well appreciated by governments in this region but not always by the commentariat is that a strong, constructive relationship with America is a vital anchor for our shared strategic and economic future. I say that not with arrogance but with a spirit of candor and respect. America is the world's largest market, with its dominant global currency and its best companies and technologies. America is making enormous investments in key areas like artificial intelligence and rare earths. On the defense side, America has the world's strongest military and makes the best military equipment at an unparalleled scale. The American defense budget is already the world's largest and we are actively seeking to substantially grow it. This is not to say you should deal only with us, and certainly not to frame our goals as hegemonic. To the contrary, we seek partnerships, not dependencies, and we understand that countries will engage widely, just as we do. But it is to counsel rejecting the delusion of fashionable but superficial ideas like middle power alliances designed to exclude America. To be clear, we encourage collaboration among allies and partners as well as efforts to build up their defense industrial capacities as part of increased defense spending in line with the new global standard set by the 2025 Hague NATO Summit. But such efforts by our allies and close partners should integrate and be complementary with America's — not vainly and futilely seek to exclude or supplant us. The watchwords should be strategies of practicality, pragmatism, and realism, not the buzzword-deep strategies of international conferences. This should come naturally here in Southeast Asia, where these attitudes are commendably habitual. Our advice to governments here in the region and beyond is to focus on the structural realities and what America under President Trump's leadership is actually doing and offering — and not on the picture that some of the commentariat paints. Of course, commentary is important and has its rightful place. But, to be frank, I think much of the commentary on the Trump Administration and what it is doing has more to do with the realm of words, symbols, and political reaction rather than actually helping us to understand reality. There are certainly many noble exceptions, but much of the conventional wisdom out there misses what is really happening. Take the issue of middle powers. There has been a lot of discussion on that issue. If you confine yourself to the commentary, you might come away with one impression. But if you look at the reality of the situation, as we advise, you will come away with another one. Thus, if you focus on words and symbols, you might think that a declaration by a group of leaders to build a new type of plane or space asset is the result. Or the convening and agreeing of a conference on increasing military strength is the result. We ourselves look at whether that plane or satellite was delivered or is likely to be delivered, and whether that platform has the required level of quality and mission suitability, and so forth. We humbly advise you to do the same. Or take, for example, the announcements of new multilateral security frameworks regarding maritime cooperation. While these agreements often generate favorable headlines, we evaluate them by a much harder but more important metric: Do they actually result in more ships in the water, expanded stockpiles of critical munitions, and genuine interoperability? A signed piece of paper or a newly formed working group does not deter coercion; fielded hard power and the demonstrated political will to use it do. Fortunately, I think my message here is already well-understood by regional governments. In fact, we see a wide chasm between the narrative described by some of the cognoscenti as compared to what we experience with governments in this region. Our counterparts in Manila, Bangkok, Jakarta, Singapore, Hanoi, Kuala Lumpur, and elsewhere — who have regular and frequent conversations with us — know exactly what the War Department has been doing. There is no confusion about our strategy and approach among those who actually bear the responsibility for national defense. They know that we are actively expanding our forward posture, accelerating the delivery of hard combat capabilities to the theater, and building out the physical architecture of a true denial defense. Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Hegseth, we are speaking softly and carrying a big stick. As Secretary Hegseth has said, we are pursuing an approach that is strong and clear but quiet. They know that we do not feel the need to engage in needless, loud, rhetorical provocations to prove our resolve. They understand that we judge strength not by the volume of moralizing speeches we deliver or the number of attendees at multilateral summits but rather through hard capability, through posture, through industrial readiness, and through the quiet, relentless strengthening of deterrence. This is both what we are focused on and how we expect to be measured and judged. And they are equally clear about what we are doing: We are putting our alliances on a sustainable, realistic, and durable footing for the long haul. When we ask our allies and partners to step up, to invest more in their own defense, and to take responsibility for their own sovereign security, we are not signaling abandonment. We are doing the exact opposite: we are inviting you to build a true partnership. This is motivated by our practical judgment that alliances are most durable when they are based on shared responsibility — mutual interest, governed by pragmatic respect, and underwritten by real capability on both sides — rather than permanent dependency. We are looking for partners, not protectorates. When our partners are strong, deterrence is strong. And that is exactly what we have here in Manila, under the leadership of President Marcos, Secretary of National Defense Teodoro, and other key leaders. We see and respect a resolute and proud nation that is determined to strengthen its own capabilities to better defend itself and its interests. A model ally. I commend the Philippines for its outstanding leadership of ASEAN during its chairmanship this year, guiding the region with a clear-headed pragmatism that matches the strategic demands of our time. And with our allies and partners throughout this region, we are actively building a strong denial defense to back up a peace through strength approach of a lastingly favorable balance of power in Asia. We are systematically strengthening our forward posture, hardening our footprint, and driving deep interoperability with key countries that are willing to shoulder their share of the burden. This is not merely about performing in symbolic exercises for the cameras; it is about fielding combat-credible forces capable of defeating real military aggression. That is what we mean by strong and clear. The proof of our success is evident in the results of our efforts in this critical region. The success of our strategy — and the very foundation of this denial defense — rests on the concrete, practical partnerships we are building and modernizing across the region, including here in Southeast Asia. Here in the Philippines, our alliance is undergoing a historic modernization, rooted in profound mutual respect. We are co-investing in resilient infrastructure, training on cutting-edge capabilities, and operationalizing our Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement sites. This is not a one-sided partnership — the Philippines is stepping up, taking the lead to defend itself, and investing more to modernize its military and coast guard. We are backing up those investments with concrete, visible support, including the rotational deployment of four Fast Response Cutters to actively partner with the Philippine Coast Guard in patrolling and securing its Exclusive Economic Zone. By strengthening our joint posture, we are ensuring that both our nations possess the hard capabilities required to deter aggression. With Thailand, our oldest diplomatic partner in Asia and only mainland ally, we are accelerating the pace and scope of our strong defense relationship. Rather than giving ideological lectures, the Department of War is focused on what practically matters to both of us: transforming legacy exercises into high-end, combat-credible training that actually tests our joint warfighting readiness and ensures our forces can operate together efficiently. We view Indonesia as a pivotal strategic actor, and we are engaging Jakarta with deep respect for its proud traditions and history. Through our Major Defense Cooperation Partnership, announced earlier this year, our relationship is growing substantially. We are focused on tangible defense modernization and deep interoperability — including through enhanced joint special forces training — that directly bolsters Jakarta's sovereign capabilities. We want a strong, independent Indonesia capable of securing its own vast archipelago. Our partnerships with Vietnam and Malaysia are compelling examples of flexible realism in action. In both cases, we leave yesterday's ideological preconditions at the door. We are stripping away diplomatic platitudes and focusing strictly on the intersection of our national interests: advancing practical maritime domain awareness and providing the hard power tools necessary to protect their sovereign rights and resist external encroachment. And in Singapore, we see the ultimate model of pragmatic, business-like cooperation. Without the need for an overarching ideological framework, we have built a deeply mutually beneficial relationship based on a clear-eyed read of the region's security environment. By supporting U.S. rotational forces, Singapore is an anchor of U.S. posture in the region, demonstrating that our presence is actively welcomed when it is grounded in shared security and economic realities rather than patronizing heavy-handedness. Across the region, from Manila to Bangkok, from Jakarta to Phnom Penh, we are pursuing ambitious, interest-based partnerships that respect national sovereignty and directly contribute to collective deterrence. Nor, I stress, is the Department of War is alone in this effort. What Secretary Rubio announced during his recent visit to Manila is a preview of the consistent and effective diplomacy our defense strategy complements. Looking ahead, let me be clear about how we will measure success in this region over the next several years. Executing a strategy of flexible realism will deliver an Indo-Pacific that is demonstrably more secure, structurally resilient, and self-reliant. Consistent with the NSS, our priority is to field a fully operational, resilient architecture of denial defense stretching along the First Island Chain. This includes robust, distributed theater logistics and prepositioned assets in the Western Pacific. We are committed to building this shared logistics infrastructure alongside our allies and partners, ensuring we can sustain combat-credible power where it matters most. Yet this defense architecture cannot rest on American shoulders alone. It must be upheld by a network of highly capable, sovereign nations that have modernized their own forces and stepped up to secure their own territory — transforming our relationships into true partnerships of equals. Because these modernized alliances will be grounded in mutual respect and pragmatic cooperation, they will be durable, deeply rooted in shared national interests. Ultimately, these hard-power realities serve a single, overriding objective: maintaining a genuinely favorable balance of power in the region. By fielding combat-credible forces, we will make aggression demonstrably infeasible and ensure deterrence is stout, resulting in a durable balance of power. This is not about empty rhetoric; it is the time-tested, historical recipe for lasting peace. And beneath that umbrella of security, the sovereign nations of this region — and the United States alongside them — can focus on what they do best: fostering the dynamic, growing economies that will define prosperity in the 21st century. Let me close by returning to the central theme of our approach: strong and clear but quiet. We will mean what we say, and say what we mean. We will not engage in peacocking or moralizing speeches. We will continue to speak softly. But we will continue to carry the world's biggest stick. We will maintain our peerless and formidable strength here in the world's key region. We will achieve peace through strength and common sense. This is the spirit we carry in this critical region. We extend our hand to work with countries throughout Asia in a spirit of partnership, respect, and pragmatism. We invite you to take advantage of this extraordinary opportunity of an Administration guided by common sense and realism, not rigidity and pretensions of moralistic superiority. There is an historic opening for us to work together more deeply and more practically. Let us seize this opportunity together. Thank you very much.

title: Boys & Girls Clubs Honor Military Youth
text: Yesterday in the nation's capital, five young Americans from across the War Department were honored as finalists during the Boys & Girls Clubs of America's 2026 National Military Youth of the Year celebration, and one walked away with the honor and the opportunity to compete at the next level. Stephen B. Simmons Stephen B. Simmons, the deputy assistant secretary of war for military community and family policy, speaks during the Boys & Girls Clubs of America's 2026 National Military Youth of the Year event in Washington, Aug. 6, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 5.18 MB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 2nd Class Charlotte A. Duran VIRIN: 260806-D-EY348-1430 Stephen B. Simmons, deputy assistant secretary of defense for military community and family policy, explained the challenges military children face and how programs like the Boys & Girls Clubs of America provide vital support to them. "At the Department of War, our No. 1 priority is ensuring America's service members are ready and able to answer our nation's call to serve," he said. "One of the best ways we can achieve that mission is by taking care of the people they love the most." Simmons is no stranger to the unique challenges that come with being in a military family. He said when he was in the Marine Corps, his family moved five times before his son turned 10. "Every time those permanent changes of station orders came in, I saw the value of our family support programs," he said. "Compassionate, dedicated professionals the world over, who helped take the sting out of those long goodbyes. They kept our kids excited about the future and made every move feel like a return home." Simmons noted that Boys & Girls Clubs of America has been an indispensable partner to America's military families for 35 years. "Wherever families are stationed, Boys & Girls Clubs are waiting for them with open arms; few organizations can say the same," he said. "Above all else, Boys & Girls Clubs promote values that America's youth need now more than ever — healthy minds and bodies, a willingness to serve and a readiness to take the lead." Each year, five finalists are named to represent youth centers in five regions of the War Department. Inspiring Youth Left to right: Fatimazahra E., Kate P., Ethan K., Patrick A. and Jonathan G. hold commemorative coins during the Boys & Girls Clubs of America's 2026 National Military Youth of the Year event in Washington, Aug. 6, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 5.96 MB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 2nd Class Charlotte A. Duran VIRIN: 260806-D-EY348-4817 Patrick A. is the Northeast Military Youth of the Year from the U.S. Army Garrison Rheinland-Pfalz Baumholder child and youth program in Germany. Although he initially grew up in Ghana, three years ago he moved to Germany to live with his aunt and uncle — both Army officers. Describing his experience as "very unique," Patrick said that because of the short time he's been in a military family, he hasn't seen the things his military friends have seen. "I only moved here three years ago, so I have never [moved] myself," he said. "But I've seen my friends PCS all the time, and I have to always say goodbye to my friends, and that's ... been very sad sometimes. But then I know that we have the youth centers and the [child and youth services] programs and [Boys & Girls Club of America] programs all around on every military installation. So, I know wherever they go, they have a safe place to go. They have a place to make friends." Patrick said he's learned about the resilience of military family life. He said he plans to study sports business in college. Kate P. is the Southeast Military Youth of the Year from Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay, Georgia. Her dad was in the Navy for 30 years, and she moved five times — from Hawaii to Maine. "As a military youth, I definitely had to move around a lot when I was younger," she said. "I had to experience a lot of different communities and adapt really quickly to many different places." Kate said it's a challenge to grow up as a military youth. "You're forced to move to these different places and experience different things that you never knew would happen," she said. "And also, having a parent who was away half of the time and not being able to see them as much during your childhood — it was kind of hard." However, she said she learned a lot about leadership. "I think I learned that to lead, it starts with listening," she said. "You need to start by listening to the people who are around you and listening to the communities that you're going to." Kate said she hopes to go to school to study engineering. Ethan K. is the Pacific Military Youth of the Year from Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada. His dad served in the Air Force for 20 years. As a kindergartener, Ethan remembers seeing his dad in uniform and interacting with other military kids. "[The military] definitely affected me because ... [I was] going to the youth center and being around kids who are also military-affiliated and having that same sense and good understanding of service and sacrifice," he said. While he doesn't remember moving, he said he does remember his dad deploying. "He was deployed when I was born, even," Ethan said. "He went to Afghanistan, Iraq, Qatar, and these would be like six-month-long deployments. So, it would definitely be a struggle in our family." Ethan said he's interested in studying biology and government. "I do hope to do the [Health Professions Scholarship Program] ... which is basically once I finish my college, I go to medical school, and I join the military then," he said. I think it just depends on each person and what they enjoy doing. I like seeing new things, even though it can be hard sometimes to adapt. But adaptability is one of the skills that we learn as military children. So, I'm grateful for that." Fatimazahra has big goals, but said that being a military youth taught her about determination and embracing opportunities. "I want to get a double degree in neuroscience and aerospace engineering," she said. "I want to get my doctor of medicine, maybe specialize in aerospace medicine and then apply to NASA and try to become an astronaut. And after that, I'd like to be a senator." title: Readout of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's Meeting With Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi
text: Today at the Pentagon following meetings in the Oval Office, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to discuss the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS, the end of the Operation INHERENT RESOLVE mission and the future of the U.S.-Iraq relationship. Secretary Hegseth reaffirmed the United States' intent to fully implement the September 2024 Joint Statement Announcing the Timeline for the End of the Military Mission of the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS in Iraq, ending the Operation INHERENT RESOLVE mission by September 30. The United States, Iraq, and Coalition partners have achieved tremendous success in defeating ISIS and now the Iraqi Security Forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, will lead the fight against terrorists in Iraq. Secretary Hegseth made clear that building a normal U.S.-Iraq bilateral defense relationship requires a secure environment free from terrorist coercion. Following more than 600 attacks on U.S. citizens and facilities in Iraq by Iran-aligned terrorist militias between February and April 2026, the Secretary welcomed the Iraq-led initiative to disarm these malign actors and to assert Iraq's sovereignty and the supremacy of its democratic leadership over all armed actors. The two leaders also discussed how a sovereign, stable, and strong Iraq paves the way for mutually beneficial commercial and defense cooperation. Secretary Hegseth and Prime Minister Zaidi agreed to continue to work together, and senior U.S. and Iraqi defense officials met subsequently for detailed discussions.

title: U.S. Navy to Christen Future USS William Charette
text: The U.S. Navy will christen the future USS William Charette (DDG 130), an Arleigh Burke-class guided missile destroyer, during a 10 a.m. EDT ceremony Saturday, August 1 at General Dynamics Bath Iron Works in Bath, Maine. The principal address will be delivered by acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao. "Serving as the shield of the Fleet, protecting the Carrier Strike Group from air and missile threats and maintaining open sea lanes for maritime commerce— this premier surface combatant will be a cornerstone of America's new Golden Fleet," said Cao. "But this warship will carry more than just advanced technology, she will also set sail bearing the legacy of Master Chief Petty Officer William Charette, whose heroic actions represent the very best of our naval service. His spirit of self-sacrifice is now permanently woven into the steel of this warship, becoming a part of the ship's culture and soul as she sails forth to defend our homeland." Additional speakers include the Honorable Janet Mills, Governor of Maine; the Honorable Susan Collins, U.S. Senator, Maine; the Honorable Angus King, U.S. Senator, Maine; Rear Adm. Matthew Case, Acting U. S. Navy Surgeon General and Acting Chief of the U.S. Navy Bureau of Medicine and Surgery; Col. Harvey C. Barnum, Jr., Medal of Honor Recipient; Michael Charette, son of the ship's namesake; and Charles F. Krugh, President of General Dynamics Bath Iron Works. In a time-honored tradition, ship sponsor, Kathryn Charette Donovan, daughter of the namesake, will christen the ship by breaking bottles of sparkling wine across the bow on behalf of her sisters and co-sponsors, Margaret Ann Henderson and Laura Charette Bennett, who are unable to attend the ceremony. Ms. Donovan will be accompanied by the Maid and Matron of Honor, Michelle Charette and Sara Charette Wright, granddaughters of the namesake. DDG 130 is named in honor of Korean War veteran and Medal of Honor recipient Master Chief Hospital Corpsman William Richard Charette. While serving with a Marine rifle company during a fierce battle for Outpost Vegas on March 27, 1953, Charette repeatedly exposed himself to heavy enemy fire to aid wounded Marines. When an enemy grenade landed near him and a casualty he was treating, Charette threw himself over the Marine to shield him from the blast. Despite being knocked unconscious, suffering shrapnel wounds, and losing his medical kit, he awoke and continued treating casualties, tearing his own uniform to use as bandages. Arleigh Burke-class destroyers are the backbone of the U.S. Navy's surface fleet, providing protection to America around the globe. These highly capable, multi-mission ships conduct various operations from peacetime presence to national security and provide a wide range of warfighting capabilities in multi-threat air, surface, and subsurface domains. These elements of sea power enable the Navy to defend American prosperity and prevent future conflict abroad. The christening of DDG 130 underscores the Navy's commitment to building America's Golden Fleet. For 250 years, American naval power has projected strength globally, operating forward 24/7, 365 days a year. This operational tempo demands continuous capability, and the Fleet of the future is our answer. Join the ceremony live stream . Media may direct queries to the Navy Office of Information at (703) 697-5342. For more information on Arleigh-Burke Class Destroyers .

title: Hegseth: Department Success Buoyed by Courage, Spirit, Leadership
text: The War Department has had a lot of success in the past 19 months, said Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. But underwriting that success is presidential leadership from the very top, Hegseth told President Donald J. Trump today during a cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland. title: Walter Reed's Skull Base Team Performs Innovative Brain Surgery
text: Complex Surgery The Walter Reed National Military Medical Center's skull base team removes a complex brain tumor from a service member at the hospital in Bethesda, Md., July 7, 2026. The team is a collaborative, multidisciplinary group of specialists who treat some of the most complex head, neck and skull base tumors. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.23 MB ) Credit: Ann Brandstadter, DOW VIRIN: 260707-D-KL921-9017 For 15 years, Marine Corps Staff Sgt. Andy Archer lived with a relentless, everyday companion — a pounding headache. "I'd wake up with a headache and go to bed with a headache," Archer recalled. He chalked it up to severe allergies or sinus issues, relying on over-the-counter decongestants to get through his demanding days. For Archer, a former drill instructor at Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island, South Carolina, and a current flight line mechanic at Marine Corps Air Station New River, North Carolina, pushing through the pain became part of his daily routine. But recently, Archer's vision began to blur. "I became nearsighted; it was bad," Archer said. "I thought I was getting old." He finally mentioned the chronic pain to his doctor, a provider with Marine Centered Medical Home New River. The doctor ordered an MRI that revealed a mass the size of a golf ball, measuring roughly 4.4 centimeters, sitting directly in front of his pituitary gland and pressing against his optic nerve. Archer needed neurological care, and he needed it fast. It was suggested that he go to the premier medical hub for complex cases: Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland. At Walter Reed, Archer consulted with Army Lt. Col. Charles Miller, neurosurgeon, and Army Maj. J. Patel, anterior surgeon, both assigned to the hospital's skull base team. The specialized surgical team mapped out an innovative, minimally invasive procedure. The surgeons planned to extract the massive brain tumor entirely through Archer's nose. "Historically, most of these surgeries were done open, which is a much more challenging procedure for the patient," Patel said. "Today, if a tumor is the appropriate size and location, open surgery just isn't necessary. Through the nose, we get the best access and the best chance of complete removal." The procedure required a highly synchronized collaboration between two experts. Patel developed a plan to navigate the complex nasal anatomy and create a clear surgical pathway. Archer had a severely deviated septum, and Patel likened the fix to "removing the sheetrock but leaving the studs" so that the nose wouldn't collapse. Once the pathway was clear, Patel used an endoscopic camera to provide high-definition, close-up visualization on a surgical monitor. This allowed Miller the crucial two-handed freedom to dissect and extract the tumor safely. "If he needs to get to critical structures, I can drive the camera closer, so he has perfect visualization," Patel noted. "Dr. Miller takes on these complex cases when many surgeons wouldn't want to risk the complications or step out of their comfort zone. My skills in navigating the nasal approach are only useful because he is skilled enough to completely remove the tumor once we get there. Dr. Miller is very well equipped to do these surgeries. It is a true team effort." In July, the team successfully removed more than 99% of the benign mass. Still, a microscopic fraction of the tumor remained wrapped tightly behind Archer's optic nerve, that if removed, carried major risks. "You must ask, 'Is it worth giving the patient a stroke or permanently changing their perfect vision just to get that last millimeter?'" Patel said. Prioritizing the patient's health, the team decided to leave that final fraction, confident the tumor is highly unlikely to return. "The biggest thing was to get the tumor out safely," Patel said. "A minimally invasive approach through the nasal passages is more challenging and we are mindful that [the tumor] has to be in a certain spot to go through the nose." To complete the surgery, the team performed a reconstruction of the skull base, using a small graft taken from Archer's leg to seal the area. Speedy Recovery Marine Corps Staff Sgt. Andy Archer poses for a picture with occupational therapist Colleen Reilly two days after the removal of a complex brain tumor at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Md., July 9, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.55 MB ) Credit: Ann Brandstadter, DOW VIRIN: 260707-D-KL921-1082 Just two days after surgery, sitting in the surgical intensive care unit at Walter Reed, there were no visible signs that Archer had just undergone major brain surgery. Archer's vision had already started to clear, and while he was dealing with expected post-operative headaches and leg soreness from the graft, his spirits were high. He and his wife, Rebecca, have been blown away by the hospitality and professionalism of the hospital staff. "The care has been awesome," Archer said, giving special praise to the nurses, as well as the physical and occupational therapy teams. Rebecca echoed his sentiments, noting that the on-campus Navy Lodge provided a comfortable, supportive environment for their recovery process. For surgeons Miller and Patel, and the Walter Reed skull base team, Archer's remarkable outcome highlights a broader mission: ensuring military beneficiaries know that they do not need to look to the civilian sector for cutting-edge medical care. "I don't think anyone else in the Defense Health Agency has this kind of team performing these complex skull base surgeries," Patel said. "Our goal is to make sure providers know this capability exists, so patients have the best options. Most patients are happy to stay in military healthcare." Thanks to an observant Navy doctor, a collaborative surgical team and the innovative capabilities of Walter Reed, Archer's toughest battle appears to be behind him. Spotlight: Military Health

title: DASW Alvaro Smith Remarks On U.S.-China Defense Relations at the PRC Embassy (As Prepared)
text: Ambassador Xie, Major General Liu, distinguished guests, and members of the diplomatic and defense corps: Good evening. Thank you for the invitation to speak tonight as you mark the 99th anniversary of the founding of the People's Liberation Army. I want to begin with the strategic vision set by my leadership earlier this year. We seek a decent peace, fair trade, and respectful relations with China. And today, the U.S.-China military relationship is stronger than it has been in years. Under the leadership of Secretary Hegseth, we are actively repairing a once-broken military-to-military channel and making clear, steady progress — as shown by my attendance here today. The Department has embraced a new approach to our military relationship — one built on candid, respectful, and clear conversations with genuine interest in de-escalation, while continuing to advance our nation's priorities. This is how two powerful militaries should engage, and over the last year and a half, we made this a reality. In the Department of War, we view the world as it is — not how we wish it to be. Our approach is one of flexible, practical realism that looks at the world with a clear-eyed perspective essential for advancing our vital national interests. As Secretary Hegseth noted in Singapore earlier this year, nowhere is this clarity more important than the Pacific — a region with profound implications for American security and prosperity. It is for this reason that our national defense strategy provides clear direction to the Department of War to set the military conditions required to achieve a lasting and favorable balance of power in the region. A region that, as a Pacific power, we cannot simply walk away from. This is why we remain committed to working alongside our regional allies and partners to defend U.S. interests. And as we pursue and defend our interests, I would reiterate that we do not seek conflict with China. We recognize that maintaining open lines of military-to-military communication reduces the risk of misperception, prevents miscalculation, and increases mutual understanding. These exchanges serve as a credible channel for crisis prevention, and we want this communication to endure, regardless of broader strategic dynamics. Over the last eighteen months, our professional engagements between defense establishments have become more productive. This progress is made possible because of the exchanges through our Defense Attaché offices and regular senior-level dialogues, including my frequent meetings with Major General Liu and my annual engagements with Major General Ye Jiang at OIMC. Their genuine commitment to executing our leaders' shared vision has been vital to maintaining positive momentum, and I am grateful to have them as close partners as we forge a new approach. Our senior leadership exchanges further reinforce this path, including discussions between Secretary Hegseth and Admiral Dong, as well as Under Secretary Colby's meetings with Ambassador Xie and Executive Vice Foreign Minister Ma. It provides vital opportunities to share perspectives, deliver candid messages, and repair a once-broken mil-to-mil channel. I look forward to continuing to build on this candid and respectful communication. On behalf of Secretary Hegseth, Under Secretary Colby, and Assistant Secretary Noh, thank you for this opportunity to articulate our approach to U.S.-China defense relations, and for the progress we have forged together. Thank you and enjoy the rest of the evening.

title: Hegseth Presents Mexican Border Defense Medal to Service Members
text: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth today recognized 50 U.S. service members — including for the first time, Marine Corps personnel — with the Mexican Border Defense Medal. 33:45 "From Day 1, operationally, this department, this building, these services rushed, surged down to the border to stop the invasion of our southern border, which is truly what it was," Hegseth said. The secretary noted that since January 2025, American troops from all services, and with a variety of skills, have been working first to gain and then maintain 100% operational control of America's southern border and to stop both drug traffickers and the flow of illegal immigration. "You have been dynamic, you have been creative, you have been aggressive, you have used the authorities you've been given [and] you work with your law enforcement partners," Hegseth said, highlighting DOW's partnerships with U.S. Customs and Border Patrol and the Department of Homeland Security. "That's why, for over a year, there's been effectively zero illegals crossing our border ... especially on the national defense areas," Hegseth said. "We decided our soil, our homeland, will be defended, and we will utilize our troops in those places to do it and give them maximum authorities to ensure that we stop the invasion of our southwest border." Mexican Border Defense Medal The Mexican Border Defense Medal is awarded to service members deployed to the U.S. international border with Mexico for War Department support to U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 839.68 KB ) Credit: Pentagon News Photo Illustration VIRIN: 260727-D-DO439-9001 The Mexican Border Defense Medal was established in August 2025. However, the medal itself is not new; it is instead a replica of the Mexican Border Service Medal from 1918. Hegseth said the reuse and reissue of a medal from more than 100 years ago is similar to the department changing its name back to Department of War. "It's a restoration, it's a reestablishment," he said. "This ... Mexican Border Defense Medal was established in 1918 to stop other incursions and invasions. And so, we're not creating something new; we actually revived the exact same medal from 1918 to be given to all of you today — as a reflection that this service is an extension; we stand on the shoulders of other great Americans who defended this nation." The secretary said those receiving the medal represent the true 1%, and they represent others like them who also contributed. "Every single soldier, Marine, and one sailor, seated here represents thousands of others who have done this mission on our southwest border and are doing it right now," he said. Their work, Hegseth said, keeps Americans safe from illegal immigration and from the poisons illegal drug cartels want to bring over the border, but are now no longer able to. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller also addressed the medal recipients, saying the border defense effort they participated in was history-making in how quickly and effectively it was implemented. "I remember distinctly, in the hours after the inauguration, the airlift had already begun," Miller said. "Massive assets were being mobilized and moved down to the southern border. There has never been in history, to my knowledge or awareness, a more radical day-and-night shift in the security posture of a country than what happened to that border between Jan. 20 and Jan. 21 ... and that was led, and driven out, of the Department of War with an urgency and a speed and a ferocity that I have never witnessed before in any other policy area that I have ever worked on." Now, Miller said, thanks to service members who are defending the U.S southern border and the actions by the president, criminal cartels who want to bring illegal drugs into the United States are no longer able to operate. "When you think about threats to the lives and security of the American people, there's a reason why President [Donald J.] Trump designated the cartels operating just meters from you on the other side of that border as foreign terrorist organizations," Miller said. Now, he said, the drug cartels are considered the same as ISIS and al-Qaida, although they operate right across the U.S. southern border, rather than thousands of miles away. "Those organizations not only export massive death in the form of narcotics to our country, but they also export sophisticated criminal enterprises whose objective is to destabilize our democracy and to end the rule of law in our country," he added. Miller said American service men and women at the border are actively involved in preventing criminal cartels from killing Americans with illegally imported drugs. "Can anybody else ask to have a more noble cause in their life than to get to wake up in the morning and know that thousands of people that you will never meet or interact with are alive today, are with their families today, are going to be at Christmas in December, and are going to be able to enjoy their kids' graduation or wedding and every other life milestone, because of the service and sacrifice that you made?" Medal recipients included 14 Marines, one sailor and 35 soldiers. Acting Chief of Staff of the Army Gen. Christopher C. LaNeve said he's proud to recognize the work American soldiers have done at the border. "I'm grateful ... that we're recognizing the tremendous importance of your service during these operations, and I'm proud that our Army soldiers are being recognized with this medal," he said. LaNeve said more than 9,000 soldiers assigned to Joint Task Force Southern Border executed 99,245 detections and monitoring operations, as well as 65 named operations, achieving a 97% interdiction effectiveness rate. Commandant of the Marine Corps Gen. Eric M. Smith said Marines conducted over 18,000 patrols and processed nearly 10,000 individual detections. They also identified and repaired over 500 border wall breaches and completed reinforcements on over 200,000 meters of wall. However, more than that, Smith said, is the dedication Marines bring to the mission. "You were asked to deploy into a complex and demanding environment, and you did so without hesitation," he said. "You were tasked with executing a mission that requires seamless integration, technical proficiency and unwavering dedication. ... You demonstrated the Marine Corps' ability to support any mission, in any [climate], in any place, with the same steadfast professionalism that has defined our legacy for more than 250 years." Following the medal presentation, Hegseth extended gratitude from President Trump. "What you've done is incredibly meaningful to the soul of this nation, and we are grateful for the service that you've given," he said. "On behalf of your commander in chief, on behalf of the nation, it is my honor to give you these Mexican Border Defense Medals and thank you for your service to this great republic." title: Boys Nation Delegates Visit Pentagon, Lay Wreath at 9/11 Memorial
text: Pentagon Memorial High school students in the American Legion Boys Nation program place a wreath at the National 9/11 Pentagon Memorial, July 21, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 245.76 KB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 1st Class Eric Brann VIRIN: 260721-D-XO220-1550 Just months ahead of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, about 100 high school students from the American Legion Boys Nation program visited the Pentagon July 21. The trip included laying a wreath at the National 9/11 Pentagon Memorial before touring the building and hearing remarks on service, character and the responsibilities of leaders. Joined by about 30 Legionnaires, counselors and staff, the delegates began at the memorial to see the 184 benches honoring those killed aboard American Airlines Flight 77 and inside the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001. Jared Harrison, a Boys Nation counselor who was a White House intern on the day of the attacks, described the uncertainty in Washington that morning and the unity that followed. He told the delegates that the country needs their leadership now. Boys Nation Navy Vice Adm. Paul C. Spedero, director of the Joint Staff, speaks to high school students in the American Legion Boys Nation program during their visit to the Pentagon, July 21, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 256 KB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 1st Class Eric Brann VIRIN: 260721-D-XO220-2166 "You have been told several times this week that you're the leaders of tomorrow," Harrison said. "I want to impress upon you: you're the leaders of now; we need you today." Brady Pace, Boys Nation's president pro tempore, connected the ceremony to the oath each delegate took as a senator. "When we as senators took our oaths of office, we swore to support and defend the Constitution of the United States," Pace said. "These souls made the ultimate sacrifice in both support and defense of our Constitution." John Alley, the program's senate secretary, spoke about the resolve Americans displayed after the attack. Pentagon Visit A high school student in the American Legion Boys Nation program visits the National 9/11 Pentagon Memorial, July 21, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.02 MB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 1st Class Eric Brann VIRIN: 260721-D-XO220-1020 "In the face of unspeakable tragedy, we did not fracture as our enemies intended," Alley said. "Rather, we came together in a way the world never imagined that we could." After two delegates placed the wreath, the group toured the Pentagon and gathered in the Hall of Heroes, where the names of Medal of Honor recipients line the walls. "It was a powerful experience," said Thomas Farrell, a delegate from Huntington, West Virginia. "The military has always seemed so abstract to me, and the Pentagon seemed like an unreachable place, but actually going and seeing where our freedoms are defended was incredibly informative." Before the formal briefing, delegates discussed their own ambitions — service academies, ROTC, aviation, intelligence, explosive ordnance disposal and other fields — and learned there is no single route into military service. They were encouraged to keep their options open and, once entrusted to lead, to listen to the noncommissioned officers and enlisted experts who have mastered their crafts. Pentagon Tour High school students in the American Legion Boys Nation program tour the Pentagon, July 21, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.57 MB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 1st Class Eric Brann VIRIN: 260721-D-XO220-1019 Navy Vice Adm. Paul Spedero Jr., director of the Joint Staff, told the delegates that the republic prospers because of leadership and service. Speaking during the 250th anniversary year of the Declaration of Independence, Spedero focused on four attributes he said effective leaders share: integrity, resilience, decisiveness and humility. "Your integrity is a currency," Spedero said. "Every time you tell the truth, even when it's inconvenient, every time you take responsibility for a failure instead of passing the blame, you make a deposit into that account. When you lie, cheat or deflect, you bankrupt it. Without integrity, you cannot build trust. And without trust, you cannot lead." The questions ranged from combat decisions and command to servant leadership, drone warfare and artificial intelligence. Asked how leaders develop, Spedero said experience matters most. "But the best contributor to your leadership development is experience," he said. "So, every opportunity that you have to be out there leading, don't miss it." The annual Pentagon visit is part of Boys Nation's weeklong program in Washington, during which delegates study representative government and public service. When asked about servant leadership, Spedero explained motive matters more than rank or status. "If you're here for rank, if you're here for stature, if you're here for money, you're in the wrong place," he said. "If you're here because you want to make a difference, and you want to make a difference with other people that want to make a difference, then servant leadership is easy." title: Army Contracting Support Enables Marine Operations Along Southern Border
text: Contracting officers assigned to the U.S. Army Mission and Installation Contracting Command Southern Border Contract Team provided contract support to Marines assigned to Company A, 1st Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment supporting Operation Ardent Vanguard. The MICC Southern Border Contracting Team is part of the Forward Contracting Element – West, Theatre Contracting Center – Americas, 410th Contracting Support Brigade, aligned under the MICC. Daytime Patrol Marine Corps 1st Lt. Everett Magnuson, assigned to Company A, 1st Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, and Army Sgt. 1st Class Devin Fuller, assigned to the 410th Contract Support Brigade, survey the terrain along the border wall as it stretches across the rugged high desert near Campo, Calif., during a daytime patrol supporting the southern border security mission. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.2 MB ) Credit: Jose Rodriguez, U.S. Army Mission and Installation Contracting Command VIRIN: 260702-D-WK488-9178 For the southern border mission and area of operation, the Marines do not have organic contracting units, making Army contracting support essential to their mission success. The Army and Marine Corps maintain fluid communication channels and continuously reach out for mutual support in joint operations. With just under 100 service members maintaining patrols around the clock across demanding terrain, Company A depends on a steady stream of support services to stay in the fight. "The Army contracting team has been instrumental to our mission success along the southern border," said Marine Corps Gunnery Sgt. Martin Hlinovsky III, a maintenance chief assigned to 1st Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment. "Their responsiveness in securing hotel arrangements that meet force protection requirements while reducing commute times has directly enhanced our operational readiness. We are extremely grateful for their contracting expertise and partnership in enabling our mission." The MICC Southern Border Contracting Team does not operate from a fixed Army post or camp. Instead, the contracting team deploys along the southern border and commutes to different locations to conduct site visits and reconnaissance for potential contracting needs. This mobile approach allows the team to be responsive to the dynamic operational environment. During the visit to Company A's operating location — a repurposed facility that presents unique support challenges — the team conducted a full review of the unit's basic life support services to assess where contracting is delivered and where gaps remain. Border Support Army Sgt. 1st Class Devin Fuller and Staff Sgt. Cody Whitlock, both assigned to the 410th Contract Support Brigade, stand watch atop high ground overlooking the border wall and surrounding terrain near Campo, Calif., during a daytime patrol supporting the southern border mission. Contracting officers assigned to the U.S. Army Mission and Installation Contracting Command Southern Border Contract Team out of Joint Base San Antonio provided contract support to Marines assigned to Company A, 1st Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, stationed along the U.S. southern border for Operation Ardent Vanguard. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.34 MB ) Credit: Jose Rodriguez, U.S. Army Mission and Installation Contracting Command VIRIN: 260701-D-WK488-9121 A key part of the visit was educating the Marines on the acquisition process and the proper channels available to resolve ongoing support challenges. The MICC team walked leaders through the fundamentals of contracting support and how they become actionable contract solutions. While these Marine-driven solutions speak to the unit's resourcefulness, they also highlight an opportunity for contracting to step in earlier so that Marines can invest their energy in the mission rather than in building makeshift solutions. Identifying these gaps is exactly why the MICC Southern Border team walks the ground. The MICC's greatest contributions have been relocating service members to hotels that meet force protection standards, reducing commute time and lessening the demand to stay for long durations in centralized or isolated locations. Specific contracting support for the southern border includes lodging and conference rooms for Task Force Leviathan across San Diego; Yuma, Arizona; El Centro, California; and Marine Corps Air Station Miramar, California. The support also includes sanitation services for Task Forces Forge, Mustang, Strike and the Army Reserve's 489th Engineer Battalion, as well as the Army National Guard's 168th Military Police Battalion and 941st Military Police Battalion units across Arizona and Texas locations. Infrastructure support includes portable office buildings, equipment rentals, wireless communications and battalion aid stations. Additionally, multilocation operations span the Rio Grande Valley, Del Rio, Brownsville and McAllen in Texas; and Nogales and Naco in Arizona. Border Partners Marine Corps 1st Lt. Everett Magnuson, company executive officer of Company A, 1st Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, alongside Army Staff Sgt. Cody Whitlock and Sgt. 1st Class Devin Fuller, both assigned to the 410th Contract Support Brigade, pause during a joint patrol along the southern border near Campo, Calif., highlighting the interservice partnership supporting the border security mission. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.01 MB ) Credit: Jose Rodriguez, U.S. Army Mission and Installation Contracting Command VIRIN: 260702-D-WK488-8588 Currently, the MICC Southern Border Contracting Team manages 19 active contracts valued at approximately $56 million in support of southern border operations. Through strategic contracting practices and effective negotiation, they have achieved $960,000 in cost savings in the past 30 days alone. Going forward, the MICC team is committed to anticipating requirements by staying engaged with the units on the ground rather than waiting for problems to surface, streamlining support for life-sustainment needs while empowering units with a working knowledge of the contracting process and the proper channels to use, and scaling infrastructure and support services to match the operational tempo and terrain. By walking the ground alongside the warfighters, the MICC team is better positioned to deliver the right capabilities, at the right time, in the right place. title: Coast Guard Monitors Chinese Vessels in the Arctic
text: The Coast Guard recently monitored two Chinese research ships as they transited north through the U.S. exclusive economic zone and over the U.S. extended continental shelf in the Bering Sea. On Watch A crew member assigned to the Coast Guard cutter Munro observes the oil tanker Bella 1 in the North Atlantic Ocean, Jan. 6, 2026. In response, the Coast Guard cutter Munro executed Operation Frontier Sentinel to actively monitor the vessels during their northbound transit. The operation was designed to protect American sovereign rights, ensure consistency with international law and position the Coast Guard to rapidly respond to any detected malign activity. While foreign vessels are permitted to operate within the U.S. exclusive economic zone and over the U.S. extended continental shelf, the Coast Guard remains vigilant to ensure their activities comply with established international laws. title: Minnesota National Guard, Croatia Celebrate 30 Years of Partnership
text: Minnesota and Croatia celebrated the 30th anniversary of their partnership through the National Guard Bureau's State Partnership Program during Exercise Combat Power 26, near Slunj, Croatia, June 29. "This partnership is best measured not only in years, exercises or official milestones, but in people," said Nicole McGraw, U.S. ambassador to Croatia. "It is measured in Croatian and American soldiers who have trained together, learned from one another and form a kind of trust that only comes from serving side by side." NATO Partnership Lt. Gen. Tihomir Kundid, chief of the general staff of the Croatian Armed Forces, and Army Maj. Gen. Shawn P. Manke, Minnesota National Guard adjutant general, attend the Minnesota-Croatia 30th anniversary partnership celebration in Slunj, Croatia, June 29, 2026. Mahsima Alkamooneh VIRIN: 260629-Z-DY230-4003 The SPP joins a U.S. state with a NATO-allied nation to strengthen military capabilities, enhance interoperability and foster long-term institutional relationships. The celebration came just days after the 35th anniversary of Croatian independence, June 25. Over the years, members of the Minnesota National Guard and Croatian Armed Forces served together in Afghanistan, trained alongside one another in Minnesota and Croatia and exchanged expertise in areas including cyber defense, medical capabilities, explosive ordnance disposal, water purification and military modernization. Thirty years later, Exercise Combat Power 26 provided another opportunity for the two forces to train together. "This exercise is more than a training event," said Lt. Gen. Tihomir Kundid, chief of the general staff of the Croatian Armed Forces, during the ceremony's opening remarks. "It is a good opportunity to exchange knowledge, share experiences and build professional relationships. Armed forces readiness has never been more important than today." title: Hegseth Hosts Iraqi Prime Minister at Pentagon
text: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth welcomed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to the Pentagon July 14, where the two leaders met to discuss the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS, the end of the Operation Inherent Resolve mission and the future of the U.S.-Iraq relationship. Anthem Salute Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi stand for the playing of the U.S. and Iraqi national anthems prior to a bilateral meeting at the Pentagon, July 14, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 1.6 MB ) Credit: Air Force Staff Sgt. Eugene Oliver VIRIN: 260714-D-VS137-9007 This was al-Zaidi's first stop on his first official trip to the U.S. since taking over as Iraq's prime minister in mid-May. "It's an honor to have you here, and I want to commend you and your team for making Washington your first destination as the leader of Iraq," Hegseth told al-Zaidi at the outset of the meeting's public portion, adding that he viewed the meeting — as well as future engagements — to be important discussions. Hegseth pointed out that the Pentagon is full of many current and prior service members who served during Operation Iraqi Freedom between 2003 and 2011, noting that he, himself, is an OIF veteran. The secretary served in Iraq while assigned to the Army's 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry Regiment, 101st Airborne Division, from 2005-2006. He told al-Zaidi that serving in Iraq all those years ago made the meeting between the two men somewhat surreal. "But it also makes me hopeful for the future of Iraq, for the future of the region and the future of our partnership as we move ahead toward security and prosperity," Hegseth said. He then credited Iraq for its own counter-terror efforts. "Like the great Americans that I mentioned [earlier], Iraqis have shed blood fighting [ISIS], inch by inch, fighting to free your country from ISIS' grip," Hegseth told al-Zaidi. Bilateral Meeting Secretary of War Pete Hegseth hosts a bilateral meeting with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi at the Pentagon, July 14, 2026. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 5.45 MB ) Credit: Navy Petty Officer 1st Class Eric Brann VIRIN: 260714-D-XO220-1589 Along those lines, Hegseth reiterated that the U.S. military is on track to be fully withdrawn from Iraq by Sept. 30, something President Donald J. Trump and al-Zaidi confirmed during a meeting earlier in the day at the White House. Despite that, however, Hegseth pointed out that Iran and its proxies in the region pose a threat to Iraq, seeking to deprive Iraqis of their choice to pursue prosperity and sovereignty. Still, Hegseth said, the U.S. will stand by Iraq now and in the future. "As the president stated [at the earlier meeting], you will find no better friend than the United States of America. … The Department of War is positioned to partner with an Iraq that chooses strength and security, not weakness or capitulation to Iran — which I know is a stance quite clearly taken by [al-Zaidi]," Hegseth said, adding that Iraq never belonged to deposed leader Saddam Hussein, al-Qaida, ISIS or Iran. "[Iraq is] a strong, sovereign country that we look forward to partnering with in a strong, mutual benefit. And in that spirit, your excellency, the United States extends that hand of partnership," Hegseth said. During his opening remarks, al-Zaidi thanked the U.S. military for its assistance in fighting ISIS in Iraq, adding that he looks forward to American commerce increasing in the region once the U.S. military mission in Iraq concludes. title: Reduction Expected for Japan Cost-of-Living Allowance Rates
text: Service members based in Japan will likely see a reduction in their overseas cost-of-living allowance in the coming weeks because of a long-term drop in the value of the Japanese yen and a corresponding increase in the value of the dollar. Yen Transaction A 1,000 yen note is passed from a U.S. service member to a Japanese civilian at Yokota Air Base, Japan, July 13, 2026. Service members living in Japan may soon see a reduction in their overseas cost-of-living allowance because of a long-term drop in the value of the Japanese yen and a corresponding increase in the value of the dollar. Share: × Share Copy Link Email Facebook X LinkedIn WhatsApp Download: Full Size ( 3.13 MB ) Credit: Air Force Staff Sgt. Skyler Combs VIRIN: 260713-F-RI665-1001 The yen recently reached a 40-year low against the dollar. Because the U.S. currency now buys significantly more goods and services on the local economy than it did previously, the supplemental allowance required to equalize purchasing power, commonly known as COLA, is shrinking. Overseas COLA is a nontaxable supplemental pay allowance designed to offset overseas prices of goods and services, ensuring purchasing power remains equal to service members stationed in the contiguous U.S. It is not a fixed pay entitlement and is explicitly designed to fluctuate with currency exchange rates. The COLA index for many installations in Japan is projected to drop to 100 and below, meaning the allowance will be zero. If that number is below 100, no pay is deducted from service members and the allowance simply remains at zero until economic conditions warrant an increase.
